subtopic: AMENDMENT OF REGULATIONS RESPECTING KILLING OF SEALS

speakeroldname: Hon. H. J. Robichaud (Minister of Fisheries):
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF REGULATIONS RESPECTING KILLING OF SEALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have stated on several occasions in reply to questions by hon. members that all aspects of Canadian sealing operations conducted off the east coast of Canada were being carefully examined with a view to bringing more restrictive regulations into effect before the next sealing season starts next March. I am pleased to be able to inform the house that new regulations to conserve the seal stocks and to ensure the use of humane methods were passed by order in council P.C. 1964-1663 on Thursday, October 29.
In view of the interest shown by many hon. members I wish to outline a few details of the new amendments to the existing seal protection regulations.
During the sealing season of March and April, 1964 newspapers and television stressed that very young seals were taken in this fishery and were killed with clubs. Unfortunately the inhumane aspects of the fishery were exaggerated by giving prominence to the few instances when inexperienced hunters did not kill the seal with the first blow. Hundreds of letters and petitions of protest were received from interested individuals and societies in Canada and the United States.
A month or two later another storm of protest arose when an erroneous article appeared in a German weekly newspaper which was widely reprinted by other European papers and, more recently, by certain Canadian newspapers. Indignation was aroused because the article stated that the seal herds off the east coast of Canada had declined from 20 million to 1 million animals during the last two years. The estimates of our scientists, based on aerial surveys and tagging experiments conducted for many years, indicate that the decrease has been from 3 million to 1J million animals over a ten year period. The feelings of humane persons were 20220-614
shocked by the statement that the animals were deliberately skinned alive in order to produce a more beautiful pelt. This statement was completely without basis.
Because of the widespread public concern I instructed officials of my department to examine all aspects of the seal fishery, including the considerable body of scientific evidence on the condition of the stocks, the effectiveness of the current seal protection regulations and their enforcement, and the methods used in commercial sealing operations. A meeting was then held in Moncton on May 20 with representatives of the Canadian sealing industry to discuss proposals to amend the seal protection regulations. A draft of the new regulations was prepared, and this was discussed again with industry representatives at a meeting in Ottawa on October 1. I then invited representatives of the major Canadian conservation and humane societies to meet with me on October 14 to obtain their views on the draft regulations. Careful consideration was given to all the views expressed by the representatives of these various interests.
The new regulations provide for much stricter control both to conserve the seal herds and to ensure against inhumane practices. To give better control over sealing operations, all vessels over 30 feet and all aircraft used in sealing will now require licences, as will all the seal fishermen they carry. As a conservation measure, the season for licensed vessels and aircraft will be shorter both in the gulf of St. Lawrence and in outer areas. To protect the mature females, which are most important for the maintenance of the herds, the killing of adults is now prohibited in the so-called breeding patches where the seals have their pups. To reduce waste it will be required for the first time that all seals killed in any one day must be landed ashore or on the sealing craft that same day.
The new regulations limit the use of aircraft for transporting sealers or skins to the gulf of St. Lawrence south of 50 degrees north, where their use is now well established, and in this area the number of young harp seals taken by vessels and aircraft will be limited to 50,000. This is an important new measure. To reduce inhumane practices the new regulations require that the clubs used

Regulations Respecting Sealing be long and heavy enough to kill at one blow, and that no seal shall be skinned before it is dead. The use of set lines with hooks for catching seals is also prohibited.
I am confident, Mr. Speaker, that these measures will assure the maintenance of the seal herds and will go a long way to reduce inhumane practices and waste. I wish to assure the house, however, that my department will maintain the closest possible surveillance of the seal fishery so that, if necessary, further restrictions can be put into force. During the coming season commencing early in March, 1965, our patrol of sealing operations by land, sea and air will be greatly intensified to assure that the regulations are observed. The results will be carefully studied.
At the request of major Canadian conservation and humane societies I shall provide an opportunity for representatives of these societies to visit the site of sealing operations and obtain first hand knowledge. After the 1965 season it is proposed to hold further discussions on the regulation of the fishery both with the industry and with the humane societies.
I firmly believe, Mr. Speaker, that these measures will maintain the seal herds and permit the Canadian industry to develop in an orderly manner. This industry is very important to many coastal communities dependent on the resources of the sea.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: AMENDMENT OF REGULATIONS RESPECTING KILLING OF SEALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure there will be general satisfaction with the announcement made by the minister, although I was somewhat surprised that he went out of his way to criticize various Canadian newspapers which in the interests of the preservation of humane methods of killing gave publicity to what was apparently gross cruelty among certain sealers though not by any means the majority of those who participate in sealing.
I want to say, too, that what is set forth in the announcement is further evidence of the beneficial effects of public opinion when aroused. All over this nation men and women in all provinces were asking for action. I am glad that action has been taken, and also that in the regulations now to be promulgated provision will be made for conservation so the industry may flourish and expand while at the same time ostracizing everything in the nature of cruelty.
[Mr. Robichaud.)

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of National Defence concerning newspaper accounts of a fire which is alleged to have taken place on the Bonaventure when in drydock at Saint John. Would the minister have any information to give the house about this matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: H.M.C.S. "BONA VENTURE"-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON FIRE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have very little additional information. As has been reported there was a fire on the Bonaventure which began in one of the refrigeration areas. Regrettably it resulted in tragedy, in that one civilian worker was asphyxiated. An investigation is being carried out to determine the cause of the fire.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Labour. Can the minister report any success in his efforts to have the maritime trustees appear before a parliamentary committee?

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: MARITIME UNION TRUSTEES-APPEARANCE BEFORE HOUSE COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there has been under discussion with representatives of other parties a motion which would refer this matter to the industrial relations committee, giving that committee the opportunity of meeting with the board of trustees. speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MARITIME UNION TRUSTEES-APPEARANCE BEFORE HOUSE COMMITTEE

subtopic: MARITIME UNION TRUSTEES-APPEARANCE BEFORE HOUSE COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have not heard a report to that effect.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR EXTENSION TO INCLUDE COOPERAGE TRADE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: REQUEST FOR EXTENSION TO INCLUDE COOPERAGE TRADE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I answer a question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg. In respect of the circumstances stated by my hon. friend affecting the cooperage trade, this is the result of a decision taken by the local insurance officer, ruling this group as not eligible for insurable employment. These persons are free to appeal this ruling to the commission itself and later to an umpire.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR EXTENSION TO INCLUDE COOPERAGE TRADE
speechtext: I have a supplementary question. Would the minister not agree that the national employment office, or the inspectors employed by that office, were derelict in their duties in that in 1959 they made no mention of these facts as presented by the minister, and in view of the fact that contributions have been accepted from the employer of these coopers since 1959 and benefits have been paid? Would he not agree that it is unfair to place this responsibility upon the coopers at this time, when it appears that the deficiency lies within his own offices?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR EXTENSION TO INCLUDE COOPERAGE TRADE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am advised that the ruling made in 1959 was disregarded by the principals involved, who continued to make contributions on behalf of these employees.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR EXTENSION TO INCLUDE COOPERAGE TRADE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a further supplementary question. From what source does the employer obtain unemployment insurance stamps?

subtopic: REQUEST FOR EXTENSION TO INCLUDE COOPERAGE TRADE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a further supplementary question which relates to the answer given by the minister to the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg. The complete disregard of the regulations in 1959 would be impossible unless the unemployment insurance offices also disregarded the regulations. Surely the responsibility rests with the department itself.

subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF LEGISLATION RESPECTING BENEFITS AND ALLOWANCES

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. W. H. A. Thomas (Middlesex West):
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF LEGISLATION RESPECTING BENEFITS AND ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a queslnterim Supply
tion to the Prime Minister. Can the Prime Minister give the house any idea what position in the legislative priority list is occupied by the government's legislation in regard to veterans benefits?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: CONSIDERATION OF LEGISLATION RESPECTING BENEFITS AND ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the whole question of program and priority is now under consideration. I hope there will be an announcement made in this regard before the end of the week.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.
Mr. Chairman, once again this committee is being asked to vote a sum, in round figures, of $740 million.
Filibuster.

The cry "filibuster" is being made already today; the same old cry by the same old gang. Last Easter we were being asked to pass a similar amount, roughly $700 million,

Interim. Supply
without debate. As you realize, we missed our usual Easter recess because of that cry "filibuster".
The people of Canada have the right to know why we are spending this large sum of money. The people of Canada, through the press, have complained that we here are not doing our duty as members of parliament. I can assure you that we are going to do our duty in this regard. We are going to consider this vast sum of money with great care. We are going to scrutinize the workings of all the departments concerned, and briefly consider the record of what the government has done during this longest and most tiresome session of parliament since 1867.
I am one of the first to admit that the legislative program during this long and arduous session has not been impressive, because the Liberals have failed to give us that leadership of which they boasted during the last two election campaigns.
The Liberals said they had the answers to our problems and would show us how to run this country if elected. Do they have the answers to the problems facing agriculture? The Conservative party when in power had the best minister of agriculture that Canada has ever had. He was the man who sold a billion bushels of grain at a favourable price, putting at least western Canada on its feet. I have very good authority for making that statement. I refer to the present Minister of Agriculture who had this to say at Falher, Alberta, as reported in the Toronto Star of October 30, 1964:
"I think the last Liberal government had forgotten the farmers during its declining years," he said. 'Til even go further-I think that on the basis of its record with our farmers, the last Liberal government deserved to be kicked out when it was."
He said the present government has continued the agricultural policies started by the Conservatives and expanded them.
I only wish they had. After the tremendous criticism of our sales of wheat to red China and other communist countries, the Liberals in fact continued to sell to these countries; but they claimed that our administration had had nothing to do with bringing about those sales and that they were the result of the efforts of civil servants and the wheat board. Now that they are selling grain to the same countries they say they did it all, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce would be the first to claim that he had had a great deal to do in this regard. It is a sad state of affairs when the present Minister of Agriculture can 
only say that it was a good idea to put his own party out, and that the only contribution he has made to Canadian agriculture has been to continue our policies. Again I say I wish he had.
Mr. Chairman, inasmuch as the hon. member-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is the minister rising on a point of order?

I am rising on a question of privilege. It is quite all right for the hon. member to quote me, but I think he should give the whole quotation where I said that "1964 is drawing to a close and it now seems"-
Order.
Make your own speech.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. That is not a question of privilege.

I will be delighted to accommodate the minister. After saying that his government had continued the agricultural policies started by the Conservatives, and had expanded on them he went on to say:
We have tried to show the same kind of concern for our farmers under the present government as was shown by the previous government. I won't take anything away from them on that score. They did things for our farmers that should have been done long before. My only objection is that they only went half as far as they should have.
That is a very good point. I will be the first to admit that we did not solve all the problems of agriculture, nor did we ever pretend to; but we made such a tremendous change that even the present Minister of Agriculture has to admit that the previous Liberal administration was completely derelict in this regard. I can speak with some authority for the people of western Canada because that is where I have lived all my life, and my constituency of Athabasca is in the northeastern part of Alberta. I can say on their behalf that there has been very little comfort in the new, expanded policy of the Liberal government. What has happened to the price of beef? What has happened to the price of pigs-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: And fowl.
-and to the price of turkeys? Not long ago the minister said he had stabilized the price of turkeys by importing some eight million pounds of turkeys from the United States.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Twelve million now.

He stabilized the price, but where did he stabilize it? At a level which has hurt not only Canadian producers of turkeys but has affected the prices of beef and pork as well. Nothing the previous administration ever did could have given the minister the idea that the way to stabilize prices was to import turkeys from the United States and lower the price so the small turkey farmer can no longer make a living. If that is the kind of action he is going to take, and this is why I rose to speak, then it is time not only he resigned but the whole government, and handed back the reins of office, especially in the agricultural field, to those who knew what they were doing.
This is not the only field in which we are lacking leadership today. On the government front benches we have a whole crowd of confused stars. Where are we going with regard to international policy? No statements are made in the House of Commons to enlighten us, but from everything I have been able to read in the press it would appear that the government is in favour of recognizing red China completely. Is this going to maintain our friendship with the United States, which alone preserves the safety of our modern world? Before we go off half cocked with a unilateral plan I think we should discuss the plan with our neighbours to the south. My position in this regard is not new. I have always favoured full co-operation with the United States, with honour.
This administration did not know where it was going with regard to atomic bombs or atomic missiles. It is not so long ago that the Minister of National Health and Welfare said it would be the sheerest folly to bring atomic weapons into Canada and the Minister of National Defence, of all people, agreed with that statement. Then the government changed around and brought in atomic weapons without any regard whatever for Canadian sovereignty. Now we have them on Canadian soil and we have no sovereignty in this regard. I understand we are now going to try to negotiate out of atomic weapons. This is a fine time to take such action. As we would say on the farm, this is like locking the barn door after the horse has escaped. We are all looking for more leadership in international affairs.
When the present Prime Minister took office he had won the Nobel peace prize. He knew how to get along with people. He knew how to get all the nations of the world
Interim Supply
together. But what does he know about getting Canada back together again? One hundred years ago the president of the United States was Abraham Lincoln, who is famous in history as the man who split rails. If we go on the way we are we will have a prime minister who will be famous for splitting Canada, and I for one want no part of it.
We are patting ourselves on the back now that we are becoming a great big grown up nation and are going to repatriate the British North America Act. How is that going to make us a greater nation? I am not against repatriating the British North America Act. As a matter of fact the British North America Act was drafted in Canada and passed by the British House of Commons at Westminster in one of the shortest debates in its history. We drafted the British North America Act, and if there is anything wrong it is because we have not lived up to it.
We need a strong federal government in Canada. Our problems are great. There is great inequality in the wealth of the provinces. Are the provinces going to opt out of all the things that are of benefit to them? I do not think so. I think it would be a retrograde step to introduce this new formula which says that two, three or any number short of all the provinces can change the basic structure of the British North America Act. If the provinces will examine the British North America Act they will recognize that it is a great charter of freedom.
Without the co-operation envisaged by the Fathers of Confederation, the founders of our country, we would have no country called Canada. We would have been absorbed by the United States at least half a century ago, probably at the time of Laurier and the free trade experiment. The reciprocity experiment did not work and we wisely threw it out. Since that time Canada has gone steadily forward. But Canada has not gone forward at times when the provinces have been selfish. Canada has gone forward when the provinces have seen themselves as integral parts of a great state, one state, one country, but a country in which minorities will always be protected.
Whenever the present government want to make a point they try to pretend that the Conservatives are the great imperialists and that we have tried to keep Canada in her diapers. I do not think so. It was a great Conservative who drew up the British North America Act in the first place in co-operation with his Conservative partner from Quebec,

Interim Supply
Cartier, a man equal in every way to Macdonald in vision, loyalty and integrity. Macdonald and Cartier would turn over in their graves today if, after 97 years of co-operation, they saw the Liberals proceeding as rapidly as they can to undo all they did and dreamed of. A formula for amendment, indeed. If the British North America Act were lived up to by the provinces and the federal government it could still be a complete formula for freedom for all people who live in Canada.
We will be glad to have the British North America Act back in Canada, because we are in fact a grown-up nation, and have been for 50 years. Great political hay was made out of this cry that the Conservatives were imperialists, and William Lyon Mackenzie King won an election back in 1926 on the phony issue that we were being dictated to by Westminster. In 1867, when the B.N.A. Act was passed, Macdonald and Cartier and all those who went over there were annoyed by the fact that the British parliament passed the B.N.A. Act without debate. They thought it was a slur upon Canada that it was not important enough to worry about whether or not we took our complete independence. As a matter of fact Mr. Bright, who was famous for championing the underdog in British politics back at that time, even suggested that they cut the strings entirely and turn Canada adrift and let her go completely on her own. Is this imperialism? They gave us everything we asked for, and more, in 1867.
The British parliament bore the full cost of defending us, and it was not until 1914-18 that Canada made that magnificent contribution which showed that she had in fact grown up and appreciated freedom under the British flag such as no other colony or nation has ever enjoyed. I think the greatest freedom has been enjoyed by those same Quebec people. We still have them with us today, and I and all hon. members know that it is a very small but vociferous group in Quebec who believe in separatism. I was very pleased to hear one of our usually loud and outspoken members say he believed that in the British crown we really have the essence of freedom. This I believe.
I think it would be a good idea if we went back to 1925 and 1926 and read again what happened at that time. I think hon. members will all realize that when we took away the prerogative of the crown to call a successor between elections and try and form a government, we lost a very, very important part of our freedom under the parliamentary system. It is possible now for a leader, not know-

ing where he is going himself, to blame the opposition for every move and to threaten parliament with an election.
Everybody knows that the people of Canada have had too many elections. They have had at least two too many, one in 1962 and one in 1963, when a vicious campaign of half truths and complete falsehoods destroyed the confidence of the Canadian people in an administration that in five short years had certainly done more for western agriculture than all the previous Liberal administrations since 1867.
Even this was used in every husting east of Winnipeg to say that western Canada was a spoiled baby. Western Canada only enjoyed what she should have always had, something approaching a fair share of the national income. I say, Mr. Chairman, that the former administration instituted these programs; the ARDA program, for example. I suppose hon. members opposite say this was their program, but it was brought in by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, as everybody knows. This is one of the reasons I said, and I say again, that he was the greatest minister of agriculture Canada has ever had. He is still full of ideas; he is still full of drive; and I know, and you know, that if he were back in that same position he would expand the ARDA program and give the maritime farmers, the small Quebec and Ontario farmers, the same hope that has regenerated agriculture throughout the west.
We hear the present Minister of Agriculture say he has expanded our program. I want to know where. It is no good talking about total farm income; we want to know how much of that income is distributed amongst the smaller farmers who need it the most. This vertical integration, the kind of legislation this government has brought in to back up the large corporation farms, is not putting one dollar in the pockets of the small farmers; and I understand from the bureau of statistics that we are losing 14,000 family farms a year.
How long can this go on; and what kind of a country are we going to have when they are all sitting in the city looking for free wine and corn oil, etc., to be produced on collective farms? The happy, small farm in Canada has always been our strength, and I want to see continued the policy of the former administration under the present Leader of the Opposition and his then minister of agriculture. He introduced the ARDA program into this house. Only under this program can the small farmers, not only in western Canada but also in eastern Canada,

derive any hope; otherwise they will be leaving the farms in even larger numbers than the present rate of 14,000 a year.
I do not think the people of Canada are interested in long winded talks about ideologies, about whether or not you like socialism. They are interested in simple things, such as can they earn a living? They were able to earn a living thanks to our government and to the policies we instituted when in office. We must go to the small farmers in Quebec and give them a chance to live and see they have the amenities of living. An automobile these days is not a luxury; it is a necessity in this country of ours. Also, Mr. Chairman,
I believe that every home in Canada should have television in order that they may participate in this great educational program that we want. That is why I have pressed for greater television coverage. So far I have not been able to get it, but I will keep on pressing for it. I do not care if I never make a name for myself as a statesman, as long as we feed the people who sent me here and improve their standard of living.
If some of our leaders would stop worrying about the history books and would get down to brass tacks, dollars and cents, income security, this country would be a great deal better off. I do not think you have to be a socialist in order to give this country security. This is the richest country in the world by far, as far as capital is concerned, when one considers what we have produced already and the potential that is ours. In my district of Athabasca 500 billion barrels of oil are there for the taking, and what are we doing about it? We started it. We should do something in this respect and get this inertia out of our policies.
We can all now say that Mr. Hees is a great man. Why? It is only because he is not in our party any more. Isn't he the same man? It was not Mr. Hees alone; he was encouraged by a whole front row of people who were on the march.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Leaving the party.

He has not left the party, and the flattering office which you people gave him did not get him into your party either. Personally, Mr. Chairman, I am a great admirer of Mr. Hees. He got this country rolling. How did he get this country rolling? It was because he listened to the backbenchers of his own party. George Hees did not think he had all the answers; he consulted us on many occasions, and if we came to him with a bright
Interim Supply
idea he used it. It was not all window dressing; he put Canadian manufacturers and Canadian products back in the markets of the world.
Then it was said that our minister of finance was a terrible man for the way he dealt with one of the spoiled boys of the party opposite. What did he do? He devalued the dollar and the present Minister of Finance wrote a book about it, "Troubled Canada". I tell the house that Canada is still troubled, and it is troubled because the government has the author of that book as Minister of Finance. The sooner we get him out, the better.
There are those who want to weaken the federal system. What about education? It is said, "Don't talk about education; that is a provincial right". Everything in this country is too hot to handle, but if the government does not handle it somebody else will. And in handling it the government should not play around with socialism.
I warn you people over there that if you continue allowing the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to make up your minds for you, he may well end up sitting in the Prime Minister's chair, because he has more intelligence than all of you put together. You have got to do what he says. You brought in a stillborn flag, but when he brought in his flag you all voted for it like a flock of sheep. If he is your leader put him in office and let's get going. If he is the dynamic leader you think, then let's have him over there.
Or why don't you have the hon. member for Villeneuve? He speaks out; he isn't silent, but 80 per cent of you people are silent whenever there is a controversial issue too hot to handle.
We are keeping our eyes on you.

You had better have your eye on me, because you will hear more from me. Your half truths and your propaganda machine will do me no harm unless you go to the people I represent and show you are doing something to help them earn a living. My people are tired of talk; they want action. Your own Minister of Agriculture admitted we took action, and he knows. He is a farmer; I will say that for Harry. He knows what has happened to the price of cattle since you fellows got in.
My people want something done about the price of farm machinery. You people brought in a bill to fix that, but I defy you to tell me how you have reduced the price of farm

Interim Supply
machinery by one cent for farmers in western Canada or elsewhere. I speak for myself. A lot of you people don't have far to go on week ends and are able to commute to your homes. Maybe that is why you are keeping the session going.
Stop talking and we will go home.

On September 8 the hon. member for Megantic moved that we stop talking about things which really do not count and get on with important legislation, but every one of you voted against that. You had been accusing us of filibustering, but on September 8 every Liberal in the house voted to continue the flag debate. You really did not want your own flag, or you would not have sent it to the committee. In that committee you had the mother of that flag sitting there. It was supposed to be a non-partisan flag, but of course that is impossible. That is why I for one never wanted the flag to go to a committee. We knew we would end up with the flag proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. The members of the committee went in knowing they were going to vote for the flag of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
Fourteen to none.

Yes, we understand how that was worked. If you want me to go through it I shall put it on the record. You brought in Hobson's choice, the devil or the deep blue sea. You voted in that plugged committee 9-4 against the red ensign and you thought that was the end of it. I have news for you.
Ten to four.

You are good at hair-splitting, but what are you doing about the price of turkeys? We can't eat maple leaves. This is not the place to talk about spiritualism. William Lyon Mackenzie King relied on his crystal ball and his little helper who is now the Minister of Transport, but we need more than that. Give the people action; then they will not be ashamed to pay you $18,000 a year. We raised our own income, didn't we?
You did not vote against it.
If you have anything to say why don't you stand on your feet and say it? Would you like the floor?

I said you did not
vote against it.
Against what?
The increase in salaries for members.

No. I think I am worth it. I can't say that you are. I backed policies which raised the price of cattle and stabilized family income on the farms. I am proud of the small part I played, and with the same amount of devotion to the Canadian people I think I could earn $18,000 a year anywhere. I am a lawyer, and I am devoting what small legal brains I have to looking through the holes in your specious arguments. I am an advocate for the people of Athabasca, and they know it. I spend 100 per cent of my time representing them, and I don't care if we have a recess or not. This is my life. I will spend 24 hours a day 12 months of the year here if you will produce some results for my people. But if you don't come up with something dynamic I will be here when you are forgotten.
If you members from Quebec want to be returned from Quebec, then do something for the little people of Quebec. Give them a chance to earn a living and share in the wonderful opportunities we have. No people ever had greater opportunities than those facing the Canadian people today. We are fighting over dimes when we should be having dollars. In some cases little, petty provincial governments are shuffling dimes around when they should be using dollars, and this is due to lack of vision and co-operation. When we have an administration that gets things done we should get behind it and stop telling lies about it. Whenever you people introduce something good I will vote for it. You are in the driver's seat.
And you are talking.

In this chamber you are supposed to stand on your feet and make your contribution. You are not helping Canada by heckling me. If you have a contribution to make I am willing to sit down and listen to it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I must interrupt the hon. gentleman to advise him that the time allotted to him has expired.

Mr. Chairman, while we are studying interim supply, and after the fashion of various members of the official opposition,
I should like to put on the record a few short quotations which are assuredly relevant to today's debate.

The first quotation is taken from Psalm 115 and reads as follows:
-eyes have they, but they see not;
They have ears, but they hear not:
The other quotation, taken from St. Luke, chapter 23, says this:
-forgive them; for they know not what they do.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Amen.
So you are innocent.

I am happy at the opportunity to take part in this debate on interim supply.
I know there are some objections to the length of time which has been consumed by this debate, but one of the duties of members of parliament, particularly members of the opposition, is to seek to guide the government along right lines through control of the monetary supply.
I think the members of the government will be ready to agree that across this country today there are a great many worried people. They are worried over the conduct of business in this house-
Hear, hear.

They are worried over the proposed imposition of a flag. They are worried over the conduct and performance of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and they are deeply worried over the proposed formula for amending our Canadian constitution and the effect it is likely to have on Canada in the years ahead.
I should like to deal first with the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Back in the thirties the corporation was set up for several purposes, the chief of these being to foster Canadianism through disseminating Canadian news, sports, educational achievements, science, history and whatever else might be going on in Canada which the Canadian people should know and which no outside news media could possibly supply to the Canadian people in the same way a national broadcasting corporation could. Its purpose was to foster national unity. It was concerned only with radio in those first years. Later on, when television took its place alongside the other media of communication, the C.B.C. arranged for the broadcasting of television programs.
Now, no organization other than a government organization could possibly provide the remoter areas of this country with radio and television facilities, particularly the latter. This was one of the fundamental purposes of
Interim Supply
the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, to provide these facilities in the remoter areas which would not be attractive to private enterprise because there would be no profit in broadcasting to those areas.
Then again, in addition to supplying these facilities to remote areas, another purpose of the corporation was to keep open and active our east-west lines of communication. We in Canada live in five regions spread roughly along the 60th parallel of latitude. These five regions are separated by areas of rock and communication is difficult. This has always been one of the problems of Canada. It has made the construction of railways very expensive. It has made construction of communicating east-west lines very expensive. But these east-west lines of communication are essential to the well-being and continuation of our national existence.
On the whole the C.B.C. has done a very good job of serving Canada. The corporation has produced some very good programs. It has brought into this country some very good programs. Nevertheless, in recent times particularly, the C.B.C. seems to be letting down its standards-I would not like to say of decency, but it is letting down its standards of, shall we say, acceptability. There is no reason why the C.B.C. should become a showcase for pornography, but there has been serious criticism of the content of some recent programs which have been broadcast over our national facilities.
I submit to this committee that nothing should be broadcast which would cause embarrassment in any way in an average well adjusted Canadian home when all its members are sitting around watching television. I submit that freedom of speech and truth should not be used as an excuse for broadcasting subjects and pictures which are ruled out in polite mixed company. In other words, if it is not lowering the standards of decency, the C.B.C. in recent times has been guilty of lowering the standards of acceptability. Acceptability cannot be defined by law; it can only be defined by public usage and by public acceptance. The C.B.C. has violated this law of acceptability.
I should like to read the committee a letter from a lady who lives in the constituency of Middlesex West. The letter is addressed to Mr. Alphonse Ouimet, Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, with a copy to myself. It says: Dear Mr. Ouimet,
I have just shut off our television set in disgust and indignation during this evening's program "This Hour Has Seven Days". If you are in any doubt as to the reasons, I suggest you check the

Interim Supply
program content. The freedom its producers allow themselves is no licence for insensible insult. There are still areas of decency.
I protest too the general terms two weeks ago of this same program during the visit of H.R.H. Queen Elizabeth. I do not know whether on that occasion Dr. Laurier LaPierre was reading from a prepared script or airing his personal opinion. In either case I was ashamed as a Canadian citizen that he. over a publicly owned medium, called into question the right of the Queen to be in Canada at all.
I would suggest, sir, that it is past time to withdraw the privilege from the opinionated individuals associated with this program of presenting their private viewpoints along with a number of very low-taste items.
Yours sincerely,
Mrs. A.G. McColl,
38 Lonsdale drive, London, Ontario.
I have before me a clipping taken from this morning's Globe and Mail entitled "Professor and cleric defend C.B.C." The article is as follows:
A Unitarian minister and an associate professor of art have spoken in defence of the C.B.C., under fire recently in speeches by members of parliament and in a strongly worded petition signed by women's groups.
George Swinton, associate professor at the University of Manitoba's school of art, said in an interview that overzealous, self-appointed spokesmen for the general public attempting to suppress truth and fact because they do not like them are vicious, irrational and un-Christian.
That is one person's view. I will have some more to say about that later.
,Rev- William P. Jenkins, in a Sunday address to nis congregation at the Unitarian church of Winnipeg, said members of parliament and a group of women were seeking, in the name of morality, to enforce a rigid censorship of Canada's most popular and penetrating medium of communication.
The defenders referred to the declaration of Canadian women, a petition circulated among women's and church groups and carried door to door in some communities, and to members of parliament's criticism of the network for an interview with George Lincoln Rockwell, leader of the American nazi party.
The women's petition said its signers aim "to end the domination of a minority who misuse the C.B.C. to spread propaganda for perversion, pornography, free love, blasphemy, dope, violence and crime".
Mr. Swinton said groups that accuse the C.B.C. of contributing to juvenile delinquency, alcoholism and immorality have not the slightest idea what morality really is.
It is the duty of the C.B.C. to show the truth and things that really exist, even though they may be unpleasant, he said. "Bigots are like ostriches with their heads in the sand. They think if they don't look at something, it doesn't exist.
He said Canadians "should be grateful to the C.B.C. for defending our freedom of opinion and expression".

Mr. Jenkins said a victory for pressure groups against the C.B.C. would mean the end of all free expression on television, a body blow to the cultural growth of Canada and a long step toward totalitarianism.
He said Canada cannot remain free unless the people face and examine the problems of morality.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I should like to comment on the suggestion that it is the duty of the C.B.C. to show the truth and things that really exist. I agree this is true, but I think all of the members of this committee would agree that there are some areas of our lives which are not to be exposed to the public view. People do not exhibit themselves when they take a bath. On nearly every toilet door in the country there is a lock. We do not wash our dirty linen in the living room. Mothers do not change their babies when there is a lot of strange company around. There are certain areas of our lives which are kept private, and it seems to me that this fact should be recognized by the C.B.C.
Surely the C.B.C. know what is acceptable in polite social circles; and surely what is acceptable in polite social circles should be respected by the corporation. Why the Canadian people has to accept some of the tripe, to use that expression, which is put over the C.B.C. networks and which is certainly a cause of embarrassment to many people, I do not know. I cannot understand the attitude of the management of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in permitting this sort of thing to continue. I think that one incident where, according to accepted standards, an improper and indecent program is broadcast by the C.B.C. is sufficient for the severest disciplinary measures to be taken against the producers of such programs. I do not know where we can start except at the top of the C.B.C., not at the bottom. Mr. Ouimet himself should be held responsible for what is broadcast on the C.B.C. networks. The producers all the way down to the bottom of the ladder should have a thorough understanding that this far out type of program, which may be acceptable to a very small minority of Canadians, is found to be objectionable and embarrassing by the average viewer of television. I say that the C.B.C. should know better than to broadcast this type of program, and everyone in the organization should understand that.
Now I come back to a clipping taken from the London Free Press for January 6, 1961, which illustrates the sort of thing to which I am referring. This is a Canadian Press report which is as follows:

Arch Oboler, controversial movie producer-director-writer, is making a film in Toronto about the Kinsey report and is using Canadian actors.
Leo G. Carroll, veteran Hollywood actor best known for the Topper series, will play the lead and will be supported by Canadians Kate Reid, Austin Willis, Sharon Acker, Toby Tarnow, Garrick Hagon and Maud Whitmore. Scenes are being shot at the grounds of the Canadian national exhibition, Malton airport and in Toronto streets and at a church.
The plot takes the form of a symposium on the famed report, chaired by Carroll. The title of the film is "One Plus Two".
Calling Canadian actors and technicians "nothing but wonderful," Oboler refused to divulge the cost of the movie but said that the film should take about five weeks to shoot.
Said Oboler: "I've written something like 700 plays, but this is the one dearest to my heart."
If ever there was a subject that was not fit for showing in the living rooms of homes in Canada it is the Kinsey report, yet we have producers who think that this sort of thing is good for public showing. I should like to stress again the point that there is an element in the C.B.C. that is going too far. It is going beyond the point of acceptability by the Canadian public.
The former government was unable to rectify this situation and the present government seems unable to take care of it. Certainly something should be done. I think when we are considering granting the government further interim supply, during which time we have the right to raise grievances and demand recourse, is a suitable time to impress upon the government the fact that this sort of broadcasting and programming must be stopped.
I should like to read a short excerpt from a speech made by Mr. Alphonse Ouimet to the Toronto Rotary club on November 25, 1960. Mr. Ouimet stated:
I wouldn't be surprised if every person in this room who follows C.B.C. programs is mad at the C.B.C. for something they saw or heard yesterday, or will be mad at us for something they will see or hear tomorrow or the next day. I would be less than honest if I did not admit that there is much that is not to my particular taste either, but I believe in freedom of taste.
Perhaps we all believe in freedom of taste, but within reason. We do not believe in unrestricted freedom of taste. If we followed that reasoning where would it lead us? It would lead us to the fringe of lunacy, indecency, immorality and everything that accompanies those things. Let us believe in freedom of taste, yes, but within reason. The C.B.C. has exceeded the limits of reason by some of its recent programs.

Mr. Ouimet then went on to say:
I don't want to labour this point. Canada, thank goodness, is not made up of 18,000,000 sheep, and we all know it.
Despite their differences of opinion, and their differences in taste, most Canadians, when they see a program they dislike, are fair enough to remember the number of programs they did enjoy. They probably also remember that the other fellow may have other preferences in programs-and that he, too, is a shareholder in the C.B.C.
Broadcasting-the kind of broadcasting we have in Canada with C.B.C.-has something for everyone.
Again we have this suggestion that there is something for everyone and freedom of taste. This freedom should not go beyond the point of reason and acceptability, but the C.B.C. has gone beyond that point.
Mr. Chairman, I do not think I need say anything further in this regard. I hope I have made my point clear and that the government will do something about this situation. There is a problem in this regard, but surely if the present management of the C.B.C. does not understand the standards of acceptability in Canada today, changes should be made in that management.
At this time I should like to make a few comments in connection with the proposed formula for amending our Canadian constitution. The suggested formula has caused grave doubt in the minds of many Canadians. I think we all believe that the repatriation of the Canadian constitution, providing for its amendment in Canada without having to refer it to the government of Great Britain, is desirable. However we do not want to weaken our nation because of our anxiety to repatriate our constitution. It is better to leave things alone than to damage our national unity. It is better to leave things alone than to prejudice our future well-being as a nation.
In 1867 two levels of government were established, a national or federal level, and a provincial level. The powers of each were clearly outlined. Under sections 91 and 92 the powers of the federal government and the provincial governments were clearly stated. The language aspect of the situation was covered by section 133. This is not a long section, and for the sake of those people who may read Hansard I think it would do no harm to put it again on the record.
Section 133 of the British North America Act, which deals with languages, reads as follows:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of parliament of Canada and of the houses

Interim Supply
of the legislature of Quebec; and both those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process in or issuing from any court of Canada established under this act, and in or from all or any of the courts of Quebec.
The acts of the parliament of Canada and of the legislature of Quebec shall be printed and published in both languages.
That is the way the language problem was settled back in 1867, and this solution has served Canada for 97 years, and has been the basis for the use of languages in this country. The problem of representation in parliament was dealt with in sections 51, 52 and others, and the admission of new provinces was dealt with in section 46. The Fathers of Confederation made a long and careful study and gave lengthy consideration to the drawing up of this act, and it has been found to be a good act.
I should like to quote from an editorial in the Winnipeg Free Press of October 30, 1964. It is headed "Present Constitution O.K." and reads in part as follows:
One of the crowning glories of confederation and of the foresight of the founding fathers has been the fact that the structure which they built has withstood these changes without being altered in any fundamental way.
The second paragraph of the editorial goes on to say:
No convincing case has been made in Quebec or elsewhere for any basic changes in the constitution. On the contrary, there is every evidence that the B.N.A. Act, a superbly flexible and adaptable document, is as capable of meeting the nation's needs today as it was in 1887. Even Premier Lesage of Quebec has conceded this.

I am delighted, Mr. Chairman, to have the opportunity of participating in this supply debate, particularly since the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration is in his seat in the chamber. This afternoon I should like to talk about Indians because I happen to have five reserves in my area, and I consider the Blood Indian reserve, being so close to it, as one of the five reserves. At least the Indians from it come over to Fort Macleod and we see a lot of them.
These Indians entered into a solemn obligation with the Queen and the federal government in 1877 at Blackfoot Crossing south of Cluny in Alberta. Over five or six thousand Indians were present, and Colonel Macleod, the head official of the federal government, attended the drafting of treaty No. 7 and the signing of it. This particular treaty may not mean a great deal to present day officials of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. I would say to them that as far as the Indians are concerned, there is nothing more sacred than the obligations they undertook at that time and there is nothing more solemn than the promises which Her Majesty's representatives made on that occasion. They sealed them by saying that as long as the rivers flow and the sun shines these obligations of the federal government would be carried out. I would remind the committee that this treaty was not made between the Indians and any minor government-any local government, or provincial government. It was made between Her Majesty's representatives and representatives of those nations which were ceding certain territory. The Indians agreed to this treaty. It took them seven days to do so. And anyone who reads treaty No. 7 can see the rights which were given on that occasion to these Indians and the benefits which the government of Canada received. To have called such a meeting as the minister of citizenship had in mind without first consulting the Indians on matters which pertain to them is entirely wrong-wrong in principle and wrong in practice. These Indians feel affronted by this type of procedure.
Under this treaty-and I have a copy of it here in my hand-the federal government promises to set up reserves. Reserves are named for the Blackfoot, Blood and Sarcee bands. A reserve is named for the Peigan band of Indians. It was to be on the Old Man river near the foot of the Porcupine hills at a place called Crow's Creek. The reserve of the Stoney band of Indians was to be in the vicinity of Morleyville. They gave $25 to

every man, woman and child in order to have the treaty signed on the occasion when they all met at Blackfoot Crossing south of Cluny in September, 1877. Our representatives on that occasion gave these Indians a solemn assurance that they would pay the salaries of all such teachers to instruct the children of the Indians as Her Majesty of Canada might deem advisable, when such Indians were settled on the reserves and should desire teachers. Well, the present government is doing that. We are providing teachers. But whenever there is any change in the treaty rights which the Indians enjoy, the Indians deserve, and indeed, as citizens of this country they are entitled to expect, that whatever government is in power in Ottawa, there should first be consultation with those who are primarily affected. First of all, the Indians should be consulted. Then the administration should obey the treaty obligations which the federal government undertook.
This treaty No. 7, I would say, was one of the worst real estate swindles I ever read in my life. What did they receive in return for ceding that entire territory? In addition to having certain reserves set aside they were to receive, the treaty says-and I shall read the committee some of the terms:
Her Majesty agrees to supply each head and minor chief, for the use of their bands, ten axes, five handsaws, five augers, one grindstone, and the necessary files and whetstones.
Well, a whetstone might have been a very valuable piece of equipment to an Indian. At the same time there is not much monetary value attached to any of these things which were given to the Indians as part of a settlement. Later, the treaty promises to give to the Indians, if they wished to go into agriculture, "two hoes, one spade, one scythe and two hay forks." Every three families were to receive one plow and one harrow, and for each band

-enough potatoes, barley, oats and wheat (if such seeds be suited for the locality of their reserves) to plant the land actually broken up. All the aforesaid articles to be given, once for all, for the encouragement of the practice of agriculture among the Indians.
As some spokesmen for the Peigans have said to me when I last visited them-and I have a great deal of contact with these Indians-it was a case of a bunch of sharp lawyers talking to a bunch of savages. That, undoubtedly, is a fair summary of what happened. In the event, Crowfoot signed this treaty and the Indians felt that in signing it they had done the right thing. They did get their reserves and they do enjoy certain rights

and privileges. One of them is that before anything in the treaty is changed the federal government must go back to the Indians and discuss the proposed change with them. It is necessary to get the consent of the people who are most concerned, and discuss the matter with them before discussing it with anybody else. This is only fair in view of the solemn undertaking into which Her Majesty entered by virtue of the agreement with these Indians.
Those who were privileged to attend the ceremony which marked the signing of this treaty back in 1877 at Blackfoot Crossing remembered it as one of the most solemn occasions in the history of western Canada. As a token of respect, Crowfoot and some of the other chiefs were brought east where they were wined and dined by the federal government. They were taken to government house. They were sent down to Montreal and Toronto and were taken around various places, and then returned to their respective reserves in southern Alberta.
My purpose in recounting this visit is because other events took place. Even if it is at the ministerial level, the idea of the federal government is to make changes affecting the Indians. The government wants the provincial governments to make these changes. But let us not fool ourselves: the Indians are a proud people. They entered into obligations, laid down their arms, and so on, as a result of solemn pledges made by the federal government. In speaking on their behalf here today I feel I am only doing what should be done and raising matters which should be understood by the minister and his staff in their relations with the Indians.
Before I close there are some other items I should like briefly to mention. I do not think I need spend any time on the flag question, except to say that some of the things I do read disturb me. They leave one with the feeling that whoever is spreading the propaganda concerning the flag might be a little more considerate of the truth, instead of creating a wrong impression of what is taking place and may yet take place in the days ahead. If the flag issue is buried, as it should be, nothing will be done and no one will be harmed. If it had not been for the Conservative party we would have today a three maple leaf flag flying throughout the country. Even the committee has indicated-

I hope the minister, for the sake of his relationships with the Indians, will give them what they deserve and what Canada as a 
nation has promised to give them. Let me repeat, so long as the sun shines and the rivers flow the rights given under these treaties should be respected, and they must be respected, Mr. Chairman.

speechtext: Is he aware of the fact that the minister made a statement recently in this house to the effect that the Indian bands would be consulted before any changes in the services provided to Indian communities are made? In view of that statement, no change will be made without consultation.

Mr. Chairman, in order to give a breather to the Conservatives who continue their marathon, and to give them a chance to charge their batteries, because it seems they intend to continue the same marathon until Friday, I will make a few remarks with respect to the doings of some people within the C.B.C. The C.B.C. was mentioned this afternoon; it is a crown corporation whose yearly deficit of $80 million has to be paid by the Canadian taxpayers, and when we ask questions of the Secretary of State about it, it is practically impossible to get any information. We always get the answer: "the C.B.C. is a crown corporation which does not have to reveal such and such information", so that it is very difficult to get any information.
A while ago I heard the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot use rather strong language in connection with the C.B.C. when he told us that there is partisanship within that corporation and that it harbours separatists.
However, the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot forgot to tell us that when his party was in office, there was also partisanship in the C.B.C. and that it is perhaps at that time that separatism started within the C.B.C. because at the time when his government was in office, there were one million unemployed in Canada, the greatest number of them in the province of Quebec.

Maybe that is one of the reasons why there are within the C.B.C. people in favour of separatism.
Are they to be blamed, or should we not rather blame those who tolerated an economic system which produced poverty in the midst of plenty for six years, while we had one million unemployed in Canada in 1962-63?
Mr. Chairman, there are shortcomings at the C.B.C., as I said time and again, there is especially a socializing group in this corporation, where parliament is treated in an indifferent, indeed, offhand manner; for those people, a member of parliament or a minister has no importance. But it is noteworthy-and Liberals as well as Conservatives noticed it, and it is not new-that as soon as a socialist from abroad visits this country, the C.B.C. presents interviews with those socialist visitors from France, Belgium, the Soviet union, in short, from any part of the world. Yet, those C.B.C. people refuse to give more or as much importance to what happens here in Canada in our own country.
At noon I mentioned an editorial published in L'Action of yesterday, signed by Mr. Lorenzo Pare. The title is:
In the caldron of Le Devoir's witch.
Mr. Pare says this:
L'Action had published an editorial giving the reasons why, in our opinion, the Queen deserved a nice welcome in Quebec. Local C.B.C. officials-
This is in Quebec city.
-asked us whether we would be prepared to express again the same opinions on the national TV network. Of course, we were. We had to get approval from Montreal, which refused to accept this plea for the Queen on the pretence that the C.B.C. avoided controversial issues.
However, in the same telephone call in which they refused a commentary on the forthcoming visit of the Queen, the C.B.C. offered us, from Montreal, to take part in a televised conference by Mr. Jacques Berque who advocates separatism for Quebec as a preliminary to the triumph, in our province, of the Marxist revolution.
In the opinion of a small C.B.C. Montreal clique the Queen's visit to Quebec was "too controversial an issue": but the separatist and communist revolution was not. The interview with Mr. Berque was taped at the Palais Montcalm, on October 2 last.
Who is this Jacques Berque? He is a bird from France: he has visited us three times in less than two years, and one visit lasted a month. A specialist in "decolonization", he has come to "sell" the French Canadians the Algerian recipe of blood and bombs. He is the one who wrote, between two trips to Montreal, that "Quebec will soon become a gigantic Cuba". He is the high priest whose words one finds, almost literally, in the Parti Pris communist manifesto, and the speaker provided for the students of the University of Montreal-
Interim Supply
-by the Marxist or socialist organization of the province of Quebec.
Does this crown corporation, which exists, thanks to the funds supplied by the French Canadian public as well as the English Canadian public, in short the Canadian people, have the right to act in this manner, to refuse that wholesome discussions be broadcast over its network while such people as this Jacques Berque are invited to appear on its network?
That is the situation. In my opinion the minister is in a position to find those who are responsible for the programs which are presented to the listeners throughout the province, to the televiewers throughout Canada.
A while ago I heard Liberal members say: Why not give us the names of the socialists with the C.B.C.? We are not even capable of finding out who is responsible for the programs in general, for this or that program. It would seem that no one person holds a responsible position within the C.B.C.
You request information from the president of the C.B.C., Mr. Alphonse Ouimet, and he dares to reply to you without even signing the letter. In fact, it is only signed with a rubber stamp.
That is the manner in which the members of parliament requesting information are treated by the C.B.C. officials. And this is why I object to these flagrant abuses.
I mentioned several times the fact that during the national news, at half past ten in the evening, the C.B.C. out of a ten minute period devotes only one and a half minutes, two minutes, two minutes and a half at most to the events taking place in Canada, inside our own boundaries, while we are told about what the socialists and communists of the world are doing.
Why not give more importance to events at home? Why not invite more regularly and more often speakers who are able to inform our Canadian people right here in Canada; in short, why not invite authentic Canadians? But no, they invite people like Mr. Berque, to mention only one.
Not so long ago another individual, a man by the name of Chartrand, of Montreal, spent a month in Cuba. As soon as he returned, he was a guest on the C.B.C.'s press conference program, to inform us that since Castro took over in Cuba the country has become an earthly paradise and all that is missing now over there is American soap and toilet paper. Imagine telling us that on the C.B.C. network.

Recently the new attorney general of the province of Quebec gave a conference or presided over a meeting of the members of the Montreal chamber of commerce. Mr. Chartrand was there and interrupted the speaker with abusive remarks.
If Mr. Chartrand or any other Canadian did the same thing to Mr. Castro in Cuba when he holds a meeting, he would be shot on the spot before he had time to break or try to break a meeting of the Cuban dictator.
They ought to be logical at the C.B.C., a crown corporation which spends every year $80 million of the Canadian taxpayers' money, instead of broadcasting programs likely to shock the Canadian people and especially the French Canadians.
The French Canadian people are not revolutionaries. They want justice in their country and they want justice from the C.B.C., whose broadcasts should be of such a nature as to inform the public and not to rouse it, as it is the case at the present time.
I have received anonymous letters from Montreal, advising me that the C.B.C. will not invite me any more to press conferences broadcast from its studios. As a matter of fact, it has been more than a year now since I was invited to press conferences by that corporation. It makes no difference to me, for I shall make use of private television in due time. But, here again, it is discrimination.
Who tells the C.B.C. to invite so and so but not to invite somebody else? We have no objection to seeing Liberals, Conservatives, New Democrats or Social Crediters invited to press conferences. But we do object to having the C.B.C. commit the most glaring and awful injustice toward the Canadian people.
Not all the staff of the C.B.C. should be held responsible. The ordinary employees are respectable men and women who work hard at their jobs. We have here in the press gallery some model employees. There is Mr. Grenier, Mr. Poliquin, Mr. Baulu, model employees who are keeping Montreal informed on what goes on in this house.
But who, in Montreal, is authorized to cut down the news submitted? Who are the responsible parties? That is what we should like to know. We want to know the people we are paying and we want to know those who are interested in presenting to us the supporters of subversive doctrines in the world. That is what we want to know: the programming authorities, and even those above them. Surely, there are some, but we cannot know their names.
[Mr. Caouette.l
When we put questions to the minister responsible in the house for that corporation, he replies that he will get information. He makes inquiries and the next day, he says: Well, nobody is aware. Thus, they pass the buck. One says it is not his fault and he passes the buck and the next one says: It is not my fault either.
There is no one responsible at C.B.C. and yet, we are sometimes presented with absolutely stupid programs, and that is an understatement. The C.B.C. must be brought back to reason and the government must see to it that the greatest importance is attached to what is going on in that corporation.
The C.B.C. is not "Radio-international," it is not "Radio-France", it is not "Radio-Cuba", it is the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
The C.B.C. should first of all be concerned with what is going on in Canada and it should inform the Canadian population on that. That is its role and it is for that purpose that this crown corporation was set up.
And let the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation at least respect the intelligence of Canadians in all provinces.
As far as French programming is concerned, let them at least respect what is happening in the province of Quebec as well as the intelligence of our people.
The C.B.C. is the organization responsible for the publicity given to terrorism in the province of Quebec.
I agree that there are separatists, that there are people who do not share the views of others; I admit that there are people who want to attain a greater degree of independence and of freedom; but they should resort to honest means and not to bombs and blood, as Mr. Berque wishes. It is not in bloody revolutions that the people find their way. In every bloody revolution, it is the people who suffer and pay with their liberty.
Mr. Chairman, the C.B.C. should be the champion of security, of freedom of the press and also of freedom of speech. On the other hand, these freedoms are not one-way freedoms. There are means of holding a dialogue, of reaching an agreement, and also there is always a means of discussing, but the C.B.C. definitely does not allow it.
Mr. Chairman, those are the few remarks I had to make regarding the C.B.C. I think that all the political parties in this house are fed up with the actions of certain C.B.C. officials.
That Montreal should dictate the policy of the corporation at Quebec or at Ottawa, we do not agree; with respect to French

programming, this is neither logical nor normal. Let those in Montreal who are unable to assume their responsibilities be removed from the positions they are now holding.
Terrorists and other persons should stop being paid to try and arouse the people or attempt to stir up a revolution. That crown corporation should stop being used to cater to the lower instincts of human nature. On the contrary, it should appeal to people's intelligence and common sense and present educational programs that will raise the intellectual level of the nation instead of lowering and depreciating it.
Mr. Chairman, so far as French programming is concerned, many are afraid to criticize the C.B.C. for fear of some kind of retaliation or to have officials of this crown corporation replaced.
Mr. Chairman, whatever threats some official of the C.B.C. may choose to make, this will never stop me from exposing evil where it exists, from denouncing such communists as may be hiding within the confines of the C.B.C., because it is not those people who are paying for the C.B.C., but the whole Canadian population. Let us assume our responsibilities as members of parliament and let us stop playing politics.
I heard a short while ago the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) blame the Liberals and suggest that they tolerate the doings of the C.B.C. The Conservative party tolerated it the same way during the six years they were in power. Let us not pass the buck but, all together, let us take our responsibilities and make the necessary changes in order that the C.B.C. may reflect a truly Canadian spirit directed towards its destiny.

Mr. Chairman, one always listens with a great deal of interest to the hon. member for Lapointe, and we did so today. I must confess that his vehemence and his emphasis do not always convince us he is correct. However, I feel that some of the points he made today indeed merit very full consideration. I cannot agree with him, though, when he attributes to the past government the programming mistakes of the C.B.C. today. This seems to me to be carrying the principle of responsible government just a little bit too far. I do not see how any government can be responsible for actions that take place after it is out of office. This indeed is the responsibility he would have us accept.
