speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I rise on a point of order, Mr. Chairman. The C.B.C. is in the constituency of St. Lawrence-St, George.

I did not say these gentlemen were not concerned with the C.B.C.. However, I believe I am still right in my contention because the only television programs available in my constituency are those brought to us by the C.B.C. These are the only programs we are able to see, so I believe I was quite correct.
The C.B.C. is of concern to the Kindersley constituency, particularly because it is one of those unfortunate fringe areas where television coverage is such that it is described by the operators as a class B or class C fringe zone. Those of you who have had experience with this will know it is not too good. As I have said before, the C.B.C. is of concern to my constituency because it is a constituency in which there is nothing but C.B.C. coverage. The private network has no coverage in the area. Obviously, for these reasons, and since we have no alternative, C.B.C. programming concerns us very much.
When we learn that the C.B.C. intends to invest $128 million in developing, expanding or consolidating services in the three major cities of Ottawa, Montreal and Toronto, we are very much concerned indeed, and I think I ought to say we are not very happy about the situation. No one, I believe, could expect us to feel other than that this is an unfair use of the taxpayers' money. It is the taxpayers' money when we, in parliament, are asked to vote $88 million this year to cover the operating deficit of the C.B.C. In this respect, I should like to quote from the Winnipeg Free Press editorial of August 13 of this year, as follows:
The financial statement of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for 1963-64 shows the continued expansion of the government owned corporation. During the year the C.B.C. received, as a grant from parliament, some $78 million; in advertising revenue, interest, etc., it took in a further $33 million, giving total revenues of $111 million.

Interim Supply
Expenses, however, totalled $115 million, leaving the C.B.C. some $4 million in the hole, over and above the $78 million subsidy it received from parliament.
More alarming to the Commons public accounts committee, however, was the sharp increase in C.B.C. capital costs, particularly those relating to the consolidation of facilities in Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal.
Those are the facilities to which I just referred.
A year ago the cost of consolidation was given as $83 million. But last month the C.B.C. president told the committee that this figure had been raised to $105 million. Now the annual report raises it again, this time to $128 million.
In other words, up and up it goes and there does not seem to be very much control.
The committee has expressed "grave concern"- and understandably-at the size of these capital outlays. It is particularly concerned at the amount of money being spent in these three eastern cities when there still remain areas of Canada that do not have adequate television facilities. Part of the C.B.C.'s purpose as outlined in the annual report itself is "By using its physical resources to bring the national program service to as many Canadians as finances allow".
Now, I would not want anyone to think that I regret spending this money. I know, and everyone knows, that we cannot have a good C.B.C. operation unless money is spent. In this country in particular where much of the service must be given to rather slimly settled areas, there is no way in which enough money can be garnered to carry the whole load. Generally speaking we feel however that in past years the C.B.C. has been doing a fine job. I think we feel also that in recent years there has been a tendency, first, to forget that all Canadians and not just the heavily populated areas are entitled to satisfactory service and, second, the C.B.C. goes to the homes-I want to emphasize that point-goes to the homes and should regard its programs in a corresponding light.
The hon. member for Calgary North, who was a member of the public accounts committee and so had an opportunity to study the accounts of the C.B.C. at some length, and who is familiar with the Glassco report, had some very pertinent points to make about the C.B.C. and its financing. I think the most important one is the fact that parliament has no practical way of controlling the expenditures of the C.B.C. We might refuse to vote the money asked for, but to me this is an impractical procedure and I feel many others feel this way too.
We suspect that in the operations of the corporation there are areas where the money might be directed to other purposes, and areas

where there are inefficiency and waste. Unfortunately there is no committee specifically charged with the responsiblity of reviewing the C.B.C.'s operations, particularly its financial operations.
True, the government makes much of the fact that it has appointed an advisory committee outside the house to bring in a report and the President of the Privy Council says that a house committee will be set up to study this report. This sounds fine, but it is not what we want. If the government proceeds no faster in this matter than it has in others, we will be discussing the C.B.C. two years from now, and meanwhile the C.B.C. will be spending in its usual, unrestrained way. This is an organization that consistently overspends its budget and it seems to say, "Why not-the deficits are paid by the people." If it were a private corporation, as the hon. member for York-Humber suggests it should be, certainly no deficits would be incurred. However, I would be one of the last to suggest that the corporation be sold to private interests. There are strong reasons why it should not be.
It is my belief that the C.B.C. is primarily an instrument of national policy. It should be a unifying force for the nation and this, with perhaps some exceptions, it has been. It should be its interest to maintain and develop a Canadian culture; and I mean a Canadian culture, not a French Canadian or an English Canadian culture. So far I have not been able to see anything especially remarkable in French Canadian culture which indicates it is worth retaining, in preference to a truly Canadian culture which we might, and indeed should, develop. However if the French Canadian wants to keep it, let him, so long as he does not want to force it down the throats of the rest of us. I am sure this is the way he feels about English Canadian culture. He does not want to be compelled to accept English Canadian culture, and I think most of us are generous enough to concede him the right that we want for ourselves.
Nevertheless, this will never be a nation if we do not develop a truly Canadian way of thinking and unify our two diverse cultures. The C.B.C. is one factor that should assist in the melding of the two cultures. I am not foolish enough to think that this unification will mean similarity. This is most unlikely, but it ought to mean a greater interchange and much more co-operation between the two parts of Canada concerned, and certainly

the C.B.C. has its part to play in that interchange. I doubt if it would play such a part if it were a private business. Indeed, if it were it seems to me we would find U.S. programming and United States events taking a disproportionate amount of the time of the medium. This would lead to even faster and greater Americanization than is occurring. Neither English speaking nor French speaking Canadians care for that. Although we may admire and respect the American way of life I think we prefer our own.
I would like to return again to the principle of one of the comments made by the hon. member for Calgary North as recorded at page 9472 of Hansard for Tuesday, October 27, when he said:
In order to deal effectively with the C.B.C. from year to year there is no question in my mind that we need a standing committee on broadcasting and a committee should be set up immediately to go into the affairs of the corporation forthwith.
There is no question in my mind either that a committee is necessary.
It is quite apparent that the board of directors does not exercise effective financial control. If it did, would it tolerate consistent overspending? Surely no board cares so little for its reputation that it would allow the company it controls to overspend year after year. This in itself is sufficient reason.
Since I have previously pointed out that my constituency is limited to the reception of C.B.C. television programs I would like to ask what is going on? I would also like to emphasize the dissatisfaction which many of my constituents, if not most of them, feel with some of the programs presented. Of course I refer particularly to the far out plays-I suppose the C.B.C. would call them artistic dramas, the sort of thing which we have been subjected to this last two years.
At once I would like to make the point that the C.B.C. is not a theatre in the accepted meaning of the term. A theatre does not have the entree to the living room of the home. No indeed, people who go to a theatre are spending the night out, if I may put it that way. They are adults, the majority of them, with fully formed characters not likely to be influenced by the licence and immorality, and the preoccupation with sins of the flesh which a good proportion of recent C.B.C. plays has shown.
People who go to the theatre choose to do so. But the t.v. sets in my constituency must be turned off if people in their homes do not want to watch the play shown. Indeed

parents may do this, but parents cannot always be in the home when such plays are shown, and the t.v. set may be running whether they want it or not. Tens of thousands of Canadians have this reaction, and the best article to state their view that I have come across is one written by Patricia Young in the July 30 edition of Our Sunday Visitor, which is the most widely read Roman Catholic weekly on this continent. I quote from the article as follows:
Recently, a prominent C.B.C. official, Mario Prizek, in defending some of the television fare that has been coming our way these days, is quoted as saying: "If you don't get some angry reaction from the public, what you're doing doesn't matter to them." I've got news for Mr. Prizek and others of his ilk who seem to have made it their cultural duty to fritter away our hard earned Canadian tax dollars "getting angry reaction." In 1951, when the findings of the Massey commission on broadcasting were made public, the broad objectives of the national system of this public corporation were given as being "to maintain a flow of information and ideas throughout the country." Information, Mr. Prizek, ideas-not a constant assault on character, patriotism and our accepted moral standards.
Of course, some perverted viewers may have an unhealthy preoccupation with homosexual prostitution, pornography and sadism, but the subjects hardly rate the morbid attention, time and money being spent on them. Take a look at a sampling of the "art and culture" being offered to us by the men who have been hired to spend our tax dollars for us. There was "Two Soldiers," a drama in the Quest series, which depicted two servicemen returning from the army. Not only were they devoid of patriotism, but mouthed the typical ban-the-bomb line and had become homosexually involved (because of their army service?) Oh yes, the public reacted angrily and the Saskatchewan command of the Canadian Legion passed a resolution strongly condemning it.
You can bet your life we're angry, Mr. Prizek- and justifiably so. Remember "A Second Look" on February 9th, which featured Ralph Ginsburg of New York, publisher of Eros and other pornographic magazines, who was allowed to defend his case on this public corporation of ours despite the fact that he'd just been convicted on 28 counts, sentenced to five years in jail and fined $28,900 for peddling his filth? Obviously, he was happy enough to come across the border and state his case. After all, there was all that taxpayers' money waiting to be spent in the name of "art and culture". Thousands of television viewers across the country were alarmed and disappointed to think that the C.B.C. with its great influence would give time to such revolting plays, which not only displayed bad taste but could be instrumental in promoting immorality in our young people.

Now I should like to refer to some correspondence I have had from my constituency. I would begin by referring to a letter which I received on October 16. It reads:
Dear Sir:
It is with deep regret that we of the Leader "Little Flower" parish council C.W.L. have to protest some of the C.B.C. presentations on television. That such scandalous, licentious, illicit, lewd, irreligious and corrupt pictures are shown is beyond our comprehension. We expect pictures of uplifting and educational qualities to be viewed on a country-wide scale.
We sincerely hope that you, our most worthy representative, will voice our opinion to the C.B.C. and trust that action will be taken to bring us films worthy and fit to be seen on a country-wide scale.
I referred this matter to the Secretary of State. He treated my request with great courtesy and brought it to the attention of the C.B.C., which replied.
As to the quality of reception in my constituency, this is something which has been of concern to us for years. I could best bring it to the attention of the committee if I were to read a letter which I have received, together with a reply on behalf of the corporation. Here is the letter I received on August 20:
I do not know if you get the opportunity of doing anything relative to our T.V. reception in this locality, but when we read about the C.B.C. spending millions on added facilities in areas where they already have half a dozen outlets, it sure does burn us up living in these fringe areas.
As you know we seldom have a real clear picture, always snow, and most of the time so bad that one can hardly make it out, this summer it seems to be worse than ever, and everybody complaining, the sound has been worse than ever, an odd time you can hear other stations butting in to say nothing of local interference.
Then there is the item of antennas. I imagine they are all 40 feet or more and hundreds of these in a town of our size certainly does not add anything to its general appearance, to say nothing of the cost of them, plus the service. With such a weak signal naturally the antennas have to be kept in good shape, regardless of their unsightly appearance.
These points are not to be laughed off lightly, especially when one sees such large sums of money being spent by the corporation in the consolidation and development of existing facilities. Again, I appreciate the courtesy of the Secretary of State in dealing with this particular problem and I should like to retail his comments briefly. He said:
Unity, Saskatchewan, is situated just outside the "B" service contour of CFQC-TV-1, Stranraer, Saskatchewan, which is a rebroadcasting station of CFQC-TV, Saskatoon, at present an affiliated station of the C.B.C. television network. The corporation does not have a television station of its own in Saskatchewan.
Incidentally, I think it is time something was done about this. I know there is a freeze at present but surely it is time for this freeze to be taken off. The reply continues:
The corporation did make an application to reserve a channel in Saskatoon and was on the verge of applying for authority to establish a station when the freeze on applications for alternative service stations was effected. It has been announced that this freeze will remain in effect until after the report of the committee on broadcasting has been received.
I believe this may be far too long. The letter goes on:
You may recall that the recommendation of the board of broadcast governors for the Stranraer rebroadcasting station was challenged in the courts by Swift Current Telecasting Company Limited, owners of CJFB-TV, whose application for a television rebroadcasting station in Kindersley, Saskatchewan, was recommended for denial by the B.B.G. At the appropriate time, if the corporation is granted authority to proceed with its plans for a television station in Saskatoon, the present Saskatoon station CFQC-TV will no longer be affiliated with the C.B.C. network. In this event, the Swift Current Telecasting Company Limited, which is affiliated with the C.B.C. television network, has given the C.B.C. and the B.B.G. notice that it will apply for authority to establish a station of substantial power to serve the Kindersley areas. In this way, the area would receive a proportion of C.B.C. service along with local and regional programs via Swift Current.

Unity, Saskatchewan, is on the fringe of the "B" service contour of this proposed station.
With these comments, Mr. Chairman, I should like to call it six o'clock.

If we are, then we had a good lesson from the Liberal party in 1962-63. He can quote figures, but the facts are that the government does not know how to run or how to organize the business of parliament and the business of the country. This has been demonstrated over and over. Does he need proof? There were the 60 days of decision; the withdrawal of the withholding tax; the fiasco of the 1963 budget; the painful orthodoxy of the 1964 one; the 11 per cent sales tax reduced to 4 per cent, upped to 8 per cent and which finally will become 11 per cent; the Canada pension plan with its "three times and out"; and the 38 pieces of legislation which the Prime Minister would have had us consider before summer recess. A Prime Minister should know more about the business of the country than that. And so one could go on ad infinitum, but I think I have demonstrated the point I set out to make, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, the remarks of the last speaker have clearly summarized the reasons why this country is facing today some of the gravest problems in its 97 years. There are grave doubts about our future expressed in every area of this nation, and these doubts do not decrease as time goes on but rather increase. They increase because people are concerned not only about the manner in which the present government is endeavouring to run the country but the manner in which it is giving away, around the bargaining table, rights which have been accepted as federal in nature and, even more than that, rights which have been accepted as necessary if we are to maintain a strong federal system in this nation of ours.
On September 17, in a press conference in Vancouver, the Prime Minister stated, among other things: "We have had more federal-provincial meetings in the last year and a half than I think in any other period". I believe that is true and I have no argument with that statement. The only realistic argument in this regard is that the federal government is taking an awful beating from the provincial

Interim Supply
premiers at the federal-provincial meetings. If we are to continue to have this type of conference, and that appears to be the case, we will end up without a federal system of government, and without a nation.
Why not get the facts?

The elder spokesman from Halifax once again is speaking from his seat. I cannot understand what he is saying, but perhaps he will get up on his feet at a later date and make some contribution to this debate. I am sure his constituents are very anxious for him to do that. I think he should make some constructive suggestions, in view of the problems in his constituency which did not exist 18 months ago.
You are well informed, sometimes.

Mr. Chairman, I come from a part of Canada which cannot afford to allow a weakening of the federal system. There is a great deal of concern in the province of Quebec about its future, where it is going and how it is going to obtain the financial assistance from the people of this nation, and the people of Quebec, necessary to run its affairs in a manner satisfactory to the citizens. If this problem does exist in the province of Quebec I suggest it is the type of problem which is of some concern to the people of that province. If that is a problem there, what must be the problem in the Atlantic provinces, which have been battling these difficulties for a much longer period of time? Those provinces received no assistance whatsoever from the federal government until the Conservative administration took office, and lost that assistance which it received for six years as soon as the present government was re-elected to office.
I have no argument about the fact that the province of Quebec has financial problems, because I believe that is the situation. That may very well be the basic reason for the unrest we have heard and read so much about lately on television and in the newspapers. I do not believe this government is giving enough attention to either the economic problems of the province of Quebec or the economic problems of the whole Atlantic area. This is of great concern to the maritime provinces because unfortunately we do not have as many people to speak for us as do other provinces. Furthermore, fortunately or unfortunately, we do not have so many unstable residents who, when they do take action to bring their problems to the attention of the 
public, do so in a manner which neither befits that province nor the nation as a whole. We in the maritime provinces try to bring attention to our problems in a sane and sensible manner. However, we have received nothing but rejection from the government of the day.
If the Prime Minister of this nation spent less time at the table with the provincial premiers giving away federal rights and more time placing legislation on the statute books of this nation, it would be of benefit to the people of this nation. We would not have the provincial premiers on our backs so often, because the people of their provinces would be more satisfied with what was being done by the government in Ottawa, and less concerned about the fact that the provincial governments need more money to take the action which should be taken in the first place by the federal government.
Mr. Chairman, it is all very well for one government to blame another for the difficulties which arise within a nation, but what we have got to face more than anything else is that, unless we maintain a strong federal system, we have no chance of surviving as a nation. It is the height of ridiculousness to talk about associated states. What we need is one nation from coast to coast with equal opportunity for all, wherever they live. There is only one way to obtain this type of future welfare for our people, and that is by maintaining a strong central governmental system.
In this nation, which really has only two rich provinces-Ontario and British Columbia -and some other provinces which were have-not provinces when the Conservatives came into office in 1957, but have had many of their ills cured by the actions of the Diefenbaker administration during those years, there is only one area that is deserving of preferential treatment as far as I am concerned, and that is the area which lies east of the eastern Ontario border. It is absolutely essential that the federal government establish policies which will be beneficial to all these provinces. That cannot be done by a weakened, vacillating government which makes one blunder after another, earning little or no respect from anyone with whom it holds conferences. That is the situation which exists today. The provincial premiers look at the federal government and at its record during the last year and a half, and say to themselves that any negotiations will be a piece of cake, because the federal representatives are diplomats and believe that diplomacy is a matter of agreeing to everything suggested. That is an illustra-

tion of what we have received from the government in the way of negotiations at the federal-provincial level.
There has never been a more realistic statement made during the past 18 months in relation to federal-provincial negotiations than that made by Premier Robarts of Ontario on October 22. Here is the premier of one of the rich provinces speaking, one of the men who is in the best bargaining position, no matter how you look at it, one of the men who has less to fear from an economic point of view from the erosion of federal powers as we see it today. Yet we find the premier of Ontario stating that he is finished with these special deals that have been going on between the federal government and the province of Quebec, that he will not countenance separation either by one province or a group of provinces and that he will not countenance the contracting out of federal-provincial programs unless there are guaranteed national standards in these fields.
From the point of view of a member from the Atlantic provinces these were mighty good words to hear. This is the type of words we like to hear spoken, because there is no hope for us in the Atlantic provinces if the present government allows this country to be balkanized as is the case at present in the propositions it is putting forward. In an article which appeared in the Toronto Daily Star of September 11 Joseph Scanlon stated among other things that $200 million would be made available to the province of Quebec on the basis of contracting out agreements which would run until 1970. He lists in detail the various programs which the government of the province of Quebec plans to contract out of and they include hospital insurance, old age, blind and disabled persons pensions, health grants, forestry agreements, campground and picnic area agreements. Some of them expire before 1970 and some of them continue until 1970.
But what a dangerous situation is inherent in this contracting out program. Where do we go when this is finished? How difficult must the financial situation of the province of Quebec be if the government of that province has to turn to this type of method to secure the finances it needs to discharge its duties to its citizens. There must be other ways. There must also be other ways in order to protect the have-not provinces of this country and to see that they are assured of at least minimum standards in every area of services.

Along with the erosion of federal responsibilities a degree of disunity has developed in this country which no one would have anticipated even five years ago. I say five years ago because I consider that period of time a good yardstick. In 1959 our Queen visited us, as she did this year, and all one has to do is to go back to 1959, recall her visit then and compare it with her visit this year. When she visited Canada in 1959 we were a happy people. We looked forward to her coming. We celebrated in a joyous manner while she was here. There was great pride in our achievements and great hope for our future.
She came this year and before she even arrived there was tremendous concern that if she did come she would never leave alive. Harsh words were spoken about her. She came to the beautiful and gracious city of Quebec, and Quebec was like an armed camp preparing for the visit of a dictator. What a change in five years. Why? Why all of a sudden have we become so disenchanted with our own country? It is strange indeed that so much could have happened in such a short period of time.
There are many things that one can point to as reasons why this change has taken place. Certainly one of the reasons is the fact that we have so many parties in the house at the present time. I think another realistic reason is found in the fact that that portion of the Social Credit party which later became the Ralliement Creditiste party decided they had an opportunity to grasp a good deal of power and influence in the province of Quebec. They developed a nationalistic feeling in that province which they cannot now control, nor for that matter does it seem that anyone else can control its outer fringes.
There is also the fact that the people of the nation could not make up their minds as to what party should form the government and they still have not made up their minds. I have no doubt that if we had an election tomorrow there would be a good deal of difficulty in trying to predict what number of seats any party would have when the votes were counted. But associated with this reason is the fact that in the election of a minority government the people were convinced they were going to get able and aggressive leadership, and instead they got a government that has been accident prone ever since it took office. I do not think you have to take my word for that, Mr. Chairman. Too many articles have been written by too many men in the press gallery who were formerly strong

Interim Supply
and devout supporters of the Pearson team as it went to the people in 1962 and 1963. The Liberals had all the answers during those two campaigns but today they neither have the answers nor do they know in what direction they are going, nor can we be sure they will be going in the same direction today as they were going yesterday.
In order to fortify my statement I will put a few short quotations on the record from a number of men who, apparently, have become disenchanted with Prime Minister Pearson and his followers. The first is Peter Newman, well known for his articles about the Conservative government of John Diefenbaker, and their attitude when in office. I am looking for the quotation and there is so much interesting material here it is difficult to find. He says:
Although there have been almost none of the brassband disasters of the Diefenbaker years, in my opinion the domestic policies of the Liberals have been a grave, quiet failure.
They just sort of rolled up their sleeping bags and died.
Then, there is this article in the Montreal Star of September 12, 1964 entitled "Mr. Pearson's Diet of Crow":
No one eats crow with nicer manners or more grace than Prime Minister Pearson.
One concludes he must like the dish, since he returns so often to the table.
The article continues in that vein and is no kinder in its treatment of the Prime Minister as it reaches the end. Then, there is Charles Lynch, oertainly not a writer to whom we could ever point as one who gave us strong support. He has made similar comments on more than one occasion. I think, from a maritime point of view, what he says about the Minister of Finance is interesting. The Minister of Finance is the one who is well known as the man who was going to solve all our problems in the maritime provinces by giving us a one way ticket out. Charles Lynch says this:
Mr. Gordon is an optimist-it would be uncharitable to call him a cockeyed optimist, after all the other things he's been called-and he really believes these new measures will work, and wiil benefit the economy, and will erase the memory of his measures to keep Canada Canadian last year, which wrecked his budget and nearly wrecked him.
These are not very kind words about the man who was one of the strong advocates of the Pearson team. These are the men about whom we are concerned, about whom I am concerned as are most Canadians, because we wonder what our future is and where we will be when we celebrate our 100th anniversary.

We have a lot of serious problems facing us in the next three years. If we could get some decisive policies from this government, if we could see ourselves going forward with programs which were in the best interests of Canada, if we could hope that they would try to shore up the powers of the federal administration at the conference table rather than continually being forced to give in and back down, if we could hope that this government would provide that type of leadership for this country they would receive our support because it would be the type of action we know would be in the best interests of Canada.
How can you stand back and review the sad story of the first 18 months this government has been in office and want to allow them to give away any more of what we have worked so desperately hard to build in the last 97 years? I do not blame Premier Ro-barts for making the statement he did in the way he did. It is like a professional playing in a game with an amateur. After a while, you get tired of winning and I would think that this must almost be the case with the provincial premiers as they sit down at the table with the Prime Minister and his cabinet ministers. They must not only get tired of winning, but they must see what is happening to this nation as a result of the fact they are winning every round. There are not many more rounds in this fight if we keep watching the Prime Minister get flattened in the ring. If he is flattened many more times in the same round, the championship will be awarded to the provinces and we will have ten associated states, but not for very long. We will become, whether we like it or not, a part of the United States of America because there will be nowhere else for us to go.
I would think the people of Quebec would be more concerned about this situation than anyone else because they seem to be so jealous of the special rights they have received under the British North America Act. Surely, they are not so unrealistic as to believe they could maintain that culture they love so dearly, and that language they love so dearly if they became part of the United States. Certainly they cannot exist as an island on the North American continent for any great length of time.

Mr. Chairman, I do not believe that anyone could accuse me of having

impeded, in any manner whatsoever, since the beginning of this session, the work of this house, if the word "work" can be considered as appropriate.
Most of the time I observed, and this allowed me to note interesting facts which explain to a certain extent the economic disarray which at the present time afflicts the people of Canada.
At the beginning of my remarks allow me to sum up some facts which one can easily observe daily in this house: approximately 50 per cent of the questions asked at the beginning of the sittings are out of order, because they are not urgent and even a great number are futile. The press gallery attracts too many members who are more interested in showing off than in looking for true solutions to the present economic problems.
In my opinion, this unrestrained pride denotes a state of mind which is incompatible with the duties and the responsibilities of a representative who must first of all endeavour to serve his electors before helping himself.
One would not need to look around very long to find illustrations of the results of such a state of mind. The flourishing speeches delivered in view of raising the dignity of the representative of the people will carry no results if the persons concerned do not attempt to prove seriously that they are somewhat conscious of their responsibilities.
In my opinion too many seem to strain their ingenuity through a verbiage which is often useless, to waste much of the time of the house, by repeating time and again, with some variations in delivery, the same things which were previously said.
I concede that, in politics, repetitions are better than contradictions. However, I have known liars who would come to believe their own lies just by repeating them often enough.
Certain politicians should be careful on that point, lest responsible observers notice that rather weak side of their personality.
I know that parliament is a place where one must necessarily expect discussions, since we are here to legislate and to amend the laws governing our land, but it is always a good thing to stick to a happy medium and I feel that one should not break too often the rules of normal limitations. Consequently, I would be in favour of any reasonable amendment to our standing orders which would make it possible for us to get practical results from our discussions.
In final analysis, that is what the Canadian people expect from us.

At present, we do not seem to find the time to consider serious legislation but that does not stop us from wasting time in spite of the fact that, in all walks of life, Canadians have to pay the taxes we levy.
I fail to understand how a certain number of supposedly serious people can be so lacking in their responsibilities to those who, at the price of great sacrifice, pay us high salaries that we do not have too much trouble negotiating. Those who claimed that members of parliament would be more interested in their work if they were well paid or better paid, must admit that the results of this session do not prove them right.
Those who are responsible for the introduction of legislation should make use of the best talents in the drafting of the various bills in order to prevent contradiction and especially to display enough foresight so as not to be faced with the alternative of having to make radical amendments as a result of pressures or discussions indicating want of foresight incompatible with common sense.
I would add that the problem is not a lack of legislation; I rather think that there is too much-it is somewhat like the flag models; we have thousands of them, but we lack determination on the means to take to adopt one.
This brings to my mind a thought which sums up a form of diplomacy in politics consisting in giving what we do not have and promising what we cannot give.
We have perhaps too many politicians who practice this kind of diplomacy; it is a cooing diplomacy which gives a great deal of expectations without any fulfilment.
The financial and economic situation in this country requires that personal political ambitions be left aside and that all people of goodwill endeavour to direct our country towards the objectives wanted by all Canadian citizens; peace, security and freedom to live in accordance with the vast potentialities of the country; this constitutes a great program of activities requiring an active and well-understood co-operation.
We have within reach a very efficient instrument of action, provided we get the loyal support of the majority of citizens of goodwill.
Among the various ways of celebrating properly the centennial of our confederation we should include, in the light of our errors and achievements, the firm determination to prepare for the future another 100 years better than those the Canadian people have

Interim Supply
lived through since the 1867 confederation, taking into consideration the facts existing now, with the knowledge that tomorrow's happening is often the result of yesterday's or today's action.
We should consider the situation of the Canadian people as a whole who have to support three governments, municipal, provincial and federal, paying taxes of all possible kinds conceived by the servants of our present financial system which is in continuing disagreement with the existing economic realities with its powers, it becomes a determining factor of the type of living the citizens of our country may enjoy.
And here I believe it is in order to quote an excerpt from a pamphlet entitled: "Merci du Communisme", written by Reverend Father Dugre of the Jesuit order. He said:
When hungry people ask for bread or for houses, should we give them a fine admonition or a house? When a young nation wants to avail itself of its vacant resources to develop, establish its sons, work for its own self, organize a fruitful life, why support it for ten years through the dole, while saving the national wealth for foreign capital?
By the way, I can say that I had personal knowledge of the famous ten year depression, and I may add that I have never forgiven the administrative system of that time for having kept us, healthy young men, ready to prepare their future, deprived for ten years of the possibility of earning 50 cents per day, or at least, deprived of the work we wished to have. And now I shall resume the quotation:
If there is a country which offers the possibility of a temporal life, it is indeed ours. In those resources challenging us, which God puts at our disposal, we should find a fuller life, or, otherwise, we shall clumsily go against the Creator's will, without being able to put the blame on Him. The fault will be that of the idle leaders, of the improvident ones, who apologize for their inertia by practicing what they call a strict economy.
Our democracy is imperfect, often hypocritical and heartless. It pays too little attention to legitimate complaints or grievances. It is too soft with important people, too hard on the little man. Such a thing ought never to happen in this young country of ours, with its potential prosperity amounting to millions which is hampered by miserable money or only meant for immigrants. There has been too much election politics. What we need is a social policy, aimed at the well-being of the family and the common good rather than for the benefit of friends and contributors to the slush funds.
Those words should make politicians stop and think, at least those who are still able to do so. This booklet is so interesting, Mr. Chairman, that I cannot help quoting another excerpt for the guidance of our planning

experts and socialist-minded people. Speaking of Russia, Father Dugre states:
Property, they claim, is being made collective, but you go ahead and try to make your streetcar ticket collective just to see who gets the ride? Communists have stretched to the extreme a calculation which is only half-right. They believed that boundless land, tremendous plants and big housing projects could save labour, heating, etc. They forgot that man is not a set of figures, but has various likes and dislikes, inclinations and aversions. And experience has also shown that 20 plants staffed with 100 men can produce more than just one plant with 2,000 employees, and with less control and more relaxation. Remember the sophism about the house being built by two men in six months; therefore, by 12 men in a month, 300 men in a day, 3,000 men in an hour and 180,000 men in a minute. It can no longer work, and yet the figures are right-
Mr. Chairman, in a civilization where the value of labour is of vital importance but runs the risk of being ignored or jeered at because of lucre, dishonesty and class struggle; charity must replace fear and compromise in the relations between management and labour if the world is to be saved from communistic materialism and if labour is to regain its true worth. It is not in the midst of constant insecurity that labour can carry out its lofty mission of feeding mankind.
Several labour leaders and businessmen begin to admit that a source of income other than the salary must be found in order to ensure a more equitable distribution of the increased production due to technological progress and developments of all kinds. Distribution methods applied up to now according to scarcity will have to be changed so as to adjust to an era of abundance.
There is an interesting article in the August issue of the Reader's Digest entitled:
Will robots control the world?
In a magazine published in 1936 appeared a summary of a study conducted by several scientists who had met in order to find a solution to the problems prevailing at that time. May I quote a few excerpts of an article by Mr. P. Barraud, an engineer:
In short, while the production equipment is work and leisure and, in this way, eliminate desti-bution have to be completely reorganized.
Therefore, there is only one problem: to distribute the actual wealth, the purchasing power, work and leisure and, in this way, eliminate destitution and insecurity. Let us keep in mind this scene of distribution among children:
10 children, 2 apples, the strongest wins;
10 children who have money, 2 apples, the highest bidder, if protected by police;
10 children, 15 apples, each his own according to appetite.
This is a symbol of the present crisis. We are acting like children.

We must restore the balance between the purchasing power and the value of consumable goods, probably through a distribution of the purchasing power based on needs and not on a piecemeal accountable inventory, or on work which no longer requires energy.
The first step will be to condemn the following ideas:
1.	scarcity;
2.	value based on supply and demand;
3.	freedom of price, work, trade and profit;
4.	capital having priority over purchasing power;
5.	domestic money based on gold.
We are not building castles in Spain nor proposing a theory, but the consequences of obvious facts.
Canadians are willing to work to manufacture goods. The government should manage to find the money, but should not take it from the needy.
It is not by looking for new terms to qualify the unemployed that idle hands will be provided with an income.
The fact that there are several kinds of unemployment: frictional, residual, chronic, or extended does not provide any income to a discouraged and inactive person.
A sound and orderly economic system geared to the needs of society must provide the necessary factors for security and should enable the people of a country as rich as ours to earn a decent living.
Production is too profit-geared and forgets that its purpose is consumption. I believe that now, during the debate on interim supply, is the time to cast an eye on the way our country is getting into debt. It would help us to see where our system is getting us.
As Canada grows and develops, the national debt increases. Under a system where new developments must be represented in dollar values, and where every new dollar is created in the form of a debt, we have here figures that are astounding. In 1867, the national debt was $93 million. In 1912, $500 million; in 1920, $3,041,529,587.
In 1939, the debt was $3,710 million; in 1947, $17,660 million, and in 1963, over $20 billion.
In the answer to a question I had put on the order paper under No. 854 concerning the amount paid in interest by the Canadian government on the national debt since confederation, we find that Canada has paid to financiers the fabulous amount of $15,287 million, from July 1, 1867 to March 31, 1964.
Mr. Chairman, imagine what could have been done in this country with this fabulous amount of $15 billion in interest only on the national debt.
When the country is in a state of lethargy, during a depression period for instance, its

debt remains stationary or increases very little. It is when the country is very active, in wartime for example, that its debt increases the most.
Any increase in the production capacity represents progress and should bring in dividends to the shareholders of Canada, to Canadians. To attain this, the government should, on behalf of the population, issue and distribute new money in order to finance new activities. But when this is left to the banks, which are lending with interest, to supply the necessary funds for progress, it is impossible, financially, to make such progress without running into debt.
We have reached a point where we do not hear any more about the possibility of paying the debt of this country, since too great a percentage of the revenue is being used to pay the interest only which amounts to more than $1 billion.
The government of this country is doing precisely what the law does not normally allow a citizen to do that is "the non-payment of its own debts".
Our wise politicians from all parties may claim to know many things, but they seem to forget that the modern monetary system is above all an accounting system and that accuracy must be its prime quality: accuracy in the outstanding volume of credit. Since this credit represents the method of payment, it is obvious that it should be in keeping with the goods to be disposed of.
The greater the number of products offered for sale, the better prepared to buy them the consumers should be, since these products are made for them. This is not the case at present, control by the banks being what it is. Money is scarce whereas products are plentiful and there are machines and hands waiting for orders to start producing. We find credit controls under various forms and we know there are so many needs to meet.
Of all the dictatorships mentioned in history, of all those at least that we are able to see in action today, the most widespread is, of course, the financed dictatorship. As soon as a country passes the threshold of civilization, it passes under a financial dictatorship.
And this kind of dictatorship has made more victims, imposed more hardship, caused more suffering, wiped out more talents, broken up more homes than any other kind. It left more moral and physical ruins than all wars, however devastating, in the history of the world.
The succession of parties in power changes nothing. It seems that governments are there

Interim Supply
to tax, impose restrictions, preach hardship, even if there is everything in the country to ensure an easy living for everybody.
This is the same financial policy imposed by the same system upon the men who are in command whether they are from one party or the other.
This does not mean that the financiers are those who invented political parties. No, but as soon as parties became established in politics, first with modest slush funds supplied by those who are favoured with public contracts, the world of finance found there an excellent machinery to control public affairs.
Electoral funds have assumed proportions-and chains also.
All financial credit originates in the bank. By monetizing the national credit on behalf of the government, by means of debentures, the banks are making of the government, whatever party it belongs to, a perpetual debtor. By monetizing the production capacity of the great corporations to which it lends the credit thus established, the banks are placing in bondage the very ones who are filling up the election coffers so as to obtain the protection of the law.
Thus it can be seen that either directly or indirectly, the banking system is placing the government under tutorship. The time has come, I believe, for the people who have the welfare of the country at heart to find another way of coping with this problem.
The present government has succeeded in securing the greatest number of members by means of American financial assistance or publicity. Goods that are subject to such a high pressure advertising campaign always find buyers in the long run, be they of good or poor quality.
In this country we have heard the words "economic crisis", brought about by the stock exchange financiers; we have had deflation, inflation, regression and you know that I am forgetting some; but when all is said and done, it is always a money problem.
The demoralizing situation in 1929 left unforgettable marks which we still feel today. The old parties can no longer count on a meek body of citizens, ready to accept their unforgivable negligence; they will have to admit that the present financial system is obsolete and that it must be replaced by a system intended to help rather than subdue human beings.
Here, I quote from a newspaper published in Montreal an item entitled "Philosophy of Life", and written by H. Louis Arbour:

One of the greatest mistakes of modern times is that stupid belief in the necessity of poverty. How many people imagine that the poor are necessary and indispensable.
If in God's creation plan there is no room whatsoever for material wealth, we believe it is our duty to state that poverty also was excluded therefrom. In his great mercy and infinite province, God gave to the earth the power and the order to nourish all his children. Material wealth belong to this world and if they are so badly distributed now, God is not to be blamed. Only man is guilty. We are poor amid a phenomenal affluence. It is up to us to organize in the best interest of all.
In a democracy, the essential function of the government is to manage public affairs according to the principles set up by the people themselves, through their representatives. It is not the function of the government to interfere in the fields of private or cooperative enterprises, to assume responsibilities which belong to the individual by right, or to interfere with the rights of the individuals, except in order to protect the rights of the others.
The purpose of a national finance system is to supply an acceptable means of exchange with an adequate purchasing power, in a free economy, to make possible the distribution of goods equal to the value of the nation's production at a given time, so that each and every citizen may get at least the vital minimum.
A major objective of any well organized society must be to help each citizen obtain by his own work the necessary financial resources to be able to get, for himself and his dependents, an acceptable standard of social welfare, without having to resort to the services of the state. When that is impossible, society must assume the cost of such an acceptable social service, so that this service can be within the financial reach of citizens.
Mr. Chairman, I conclude my remarks by quoting this thought of the founder of the distributive economic doctrine of social credit, Major Douglas:
Social Credit is a new strategy for an old battle, between the tyrant's will to dominate and the individual's will for freedom.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on this debate on interim supply I want to refer to a question which I believe will be one of greatest importance in the history of Canada, namely the question of the relationship of the federal government to the provincial governments. I propose to divide my discussion into four general parts under the following headings: (1) federal-provincial fiscal arrangements; (2) co-operative federal-

ism and the process of opting out; (3) proposed amendments to the British North America Act; (4) unilateral provincial action to create barriers along provincial boundaries.
First then, Mr. Chairman, with regard to federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, we have a revenue pie, and the question arises as to how this pie should be divided between the federal government and the provincial governments. One could further ask how the local governments should receive their share. It is largely, though in my opinion not exclusively, the responsibility of the provincial governments to say what share of this revenue pie the local governments shall receive.
Mr. Chairman, perhaps I should make a few comments about what has happened in recent years with regard to the splitting of this revenue pie as between the federal and provincial governments. The British North America Act delegates or gives to each of the federal and provincial governments certain rights of taxation. Early in the war, I believe in 1941, by agreement the provincial governments gave up to the federal government the important rights of direct taxation, particularly in respect to income tax.
Let us consider what the federal government has paid to the provincial governments in recent years. In the fiscal year 1956-57, for example, the payments by the federal government to the provincial governments amounted to some $689 million. This amount increased in the fiscal year 1961-62 to $1,500 million, which is more than double what was paid in the fiscal year 1956-57. Those were years in which the previous government was in power.
I remember very well how that government was blamed for operating under large budgetary deficits. The fact is that if there had not been an increase in the payments to provincial governments there would not have been federal budgetary deficits during those years. There was no thanks given to the federal government of that time for those increased payments to the provinces. As a matter of fact, the government of that day was blamed for the large deficits it was incurring. This trend has been continued by the present government.
In the fiscal year 1963-64 the payments by the federal government to the provincial governments amounted to $1,900 million. Just recently, under the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Revision Act, a further increase was made by the present government in the payments to the provincial governments. In 1964-65 there is to be an increase in those payments to the extent of some $87 million. In the
Interim Supply
fiscal year 1965-66 there is to be an increase in the payments of $167 million. In the fiscal year 1966-67 there is to be an increase of $264 million.
I refer to these figures, and the recent Federal-Provincial Fiscal Revision Act because of the interesting feature that appears in this legislation in respect of the distribution of these payments paid by the federal government to the various provinces.
When the previous government introduced the equalization formula it was designed to help the have-not provinces. Those provinces generally are conceded to be the four provinces of Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. Under the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Revision Act, passed a few months ago, that trend seems to have been changed. Under that provision the total sum of $218 million, in round figures, is to be paid to the provinces in the three years ending 1966-67. Of that amount some $136 million, or 61 per cent, is to be paid to one province, which is not one of the four have-not provinces. Those provinces receive a total of $44 million, which represents 20 per cent of the equalization payments under this provision. I mention that fact only as an aside. My main theme is, how is the revenue pie being divided between federal and provincial governments?
What should the test or criterion be as to which government, federal or provincial, needs the biggest slice of this revenue pie? It seems to me as a layman that one of the criteria that might be used is the extent to which each of these governments has a budgetary surplus or deficit. Quite often a government, such as the federal or provincial governments, will have a planned budgetary deficit for political reasons. However, in general terms it seems to me that the extent to which the expenditures of the government exceed its revenue is a good indication of the need of that government, and the extent to which that government feels it can increase taxation so as to increase its revenue.
Let us take a look at the deficits of the provincial governments as compared to the deficits of the federal government in recent years. In the five year period, 1960 to 1964, the combined budgetary deficits of the provincial governments amounted to some $12 billion. In the same period of time the budgetary deficits of the federal government amounted to some $29 billion. That is more than twice the combined deficits of the provincial governments. One might ask, what does twice

Interim Supply
the deficit mean? I have tried to relate the deficits of the provincial governments to the deficit of the federal government by relating them to the total revenue of those governments.
Expressing provincial deficits, for a four year period, as a percentage of the revenue available to the provincial governments, we find that the deficits amount to about 8 per cent; whereas in the case of the federal government, the deficits in relation to the revenues amount to over 8 per cent. My contention is that when it comes to splitting up the revenue pie between federal and provincial governments, the provincial governments have had their share.
In 1961 Hon. Donald Fleming, who was then the minister of finance, told us that during the federal-provincial conference held late in 1960 the provincial representatives to those conferences put their demands to the federal government, and that if the federal government had acceded to those demands it would have had to pay out some $2 billion each year in order to satisfy the provincial governments.
It is traditional that provincial governments place more and more demands upon the federal government, but the question is, how should this revenue pie be divided among the federal and provincial governments. A further question then arises as to what are the proper responsibilities of each of these levels of government.
I call to mind what the premier of British Columbia said in a brief he presented to the federal government late in 1960. He said that the proper source of revenue to finance education was income tax. At that time the provinces had given up their rights in respect of income taxes, by way of agreement. In 1961, under the new arrangements made by the previous government, that right was returned to the provinces, allowing them to levy income taxes. After the premier of British Columbia had received the right again to levy income taxes, no longer was this a proper source of revenue to finance education.
We then come to the question as to what are the responsibilities of the federal government compared with those of the provincial governments. Certainly the provincial governments have major problems but it seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that there are certain questions which, although under our constitution they might properly be provincial responsibilities, are problems that can be solved only by either direct or indirect
[Mr. Chatterton.l
federal action, and this certainly involves federal expenditure.
I have in mind, for example, higher education. Late last year the Canadian universities foundation requested that the federal government make available the sum of $300 million in matching capital grants. There is the question of northern development. There is the problem of the urbanization of Canada. In my opinion one of the major questions that will face Canada in the next quarter of a century will be what is to be done to solve the problems created by people moving into the metropolitan areas. Certainly the actions that federal governments have taken to date with regard to urban renewal have merely scratched the surface.
Another federal responsibility that will have to be faced is medicare. There is the question of water resource development across our country and the question of a transcontinental power grid. There are innumerable questions such as these that obviously have to be tackled by the federal government, although they may not be clearly its responsibility under the constitution. Therefore there has to be a reappraisal of the position of the federal government in relation to the provincial governments in so far as the division of revenue is concerned, and it seems to me that the premier of the province of Manitoba put his finger on the right spot when he said that there should be a clear definition of priorities in so far as the federal and provincial governments are concerned.
The next heading I want to deal with under the general question of federal-provincial relations is that of the so-called co-operative federalism or opting out process. Throughout the world today there is a trend promoted by necessity for governing bodies to get together and through a more central organization solve the problems which are common to the lesser parts. A good example of this is the creation of the common market, but even in Africa there is a general movement, though a halting one, of the emerging countries to get together to see whether in a co-operative fashion they can solve the problems that each of these countries faces.
It seems to me that today in Canada the trend is in the other direction. I know it is said frequently that Canada is a country of widely differing parts and therefore it is necessary for each of these differing parts to have a large measure of autonomy. The fact is that Canada is a difficult country to govern, largely because of the differences of

geography of its parts, but also because of ethnic differences; but by the same argument I think it is essential that the central government introduce a certain measure of equal opportunity in every sector of these differing parts of Canada.
When we are considering the problem of opting out, co-operative federalism and the relation of citizens of Canada to their provinces and the federal government the question arises, which am I first? Am I first of all a Canadian and second a provincial? I believe the hon. member for Queens raised this question in his very thoughtful speech a couple of days ago, and this brings me to what seems to be a problem in at least one of our provinces. I refer to a speech made by the Minister of Justice on October 20, 1964, before the chamber of commerce of the district of Montreal. As found on page 9 of the released text of the minister's speech, he is talking about the position of the members of parliament from the province of Quebec, whether there is a difference in loyalty, and he said:
How, in practice, do these members of parliament reconcile their double loyalty as Quebeckers and Canadians? They do so by realizing that the cultural ideal incarnate in Quebec does not deny the political ideal incarnate in Canada. My colleagues and I are, to begin with, French Canadians; we seek intransigently the free flowering of French civilization from sea to sea, beginning with the province of our birth.
The words I want to emphasize in this quotation are:
My colleagues and I are, to begin with, French Canadians.
It is this question of emphasis as to what I am first which it seems to me creates the problem in Canada today. The Minister of Justice seems to feel that he is first of all a provincial. Should I say that I am first of all a British Columbian and then a Canadian, or should I say I am first of all an English Canadian and then a Canadian? In my opinion there should be no question that we are first of all Canadians, and then after that we can offer our allegiance to our provinces or our municipalities or our ridings or whatever it may be.
There is a trend recently in Canada toward the decentralization of power from the federal government to the provincial governments. When I speak of centralization I am not referring to bureaucracy. Under the present government there is also a growing trend toward increasing control and increasing bureaucracy. For instance, in the d.b.s. bulletin for October 30, 1964 some
Interim Supply
figures are given with regard to federal government employment. The government of Canada together with its corporations and agencies employed some 341,153 persons as of May 31 this year, which is an increase of 2,619 from May, 1963. The bulletin goes on to point out that the increase in cost is some $20 million for five months of the year or some $50 million per year. This is a different kind of centralization. This is what I would call the growth of bureaucracy, and certainly it is a trend away from what the Glassco commission recommended.
But what I mean when I refer to centralization or decentralization is the division of powers between the federal and provincial governments.
In this regard, Mr. Chairman, I should like to quote from the Vancouver Province of October 6, 1964. This editorial is headlined, "One More Strike and They're Out". I quote:
Any government can make a mistake and, through public forgetfulness or forgiveness, expect to survive. But when a government-such as the present Liberal administration in Ottawa *-makes blunder after ghastly blunder, its life expectancy becomes precarious.
This could explain why the government is under pressure from some of its supporters to take a tougher line with the provinces in a series of constitutional and tax talks which start in the capital this week.
If Mr. Pearson and his advisers fritter away much more national authority by allowing the provinces to "opt out" of more national programs they can endanger the whole fabric of Canadian unity. Such weakness might be the last straw for the government, a minority government that holds office only at the pleasure of splinter groups in the House of Commons.
I skip part of the editorial and read another paragraph:
Little more need be said about Mr. Pearson's so far unsuccessful effort to impose a new flag on the country. His misguided plan to promote greater national unity with his maple leaf banner has inflamed the most violent regional quarrel in years. It brought parliament to a standstill for more than three weeks and is still unresolved.
This, Mr. Chairman, indicates how editorial writers across the country feel with regard to this so-called co-operative federalism of the present government. There are one or two instances recently which I could cite relating to acts passed by this parliament. One is the Canada Student Loans Act, a piece of legislation that was excellent in its intent but I believe the Minister of Finance will find out when he has completed his investigation that serious weaknesses have shown up in the administration of this act. This results almost entirely from the fact the administra-

Interim Supply
tion was left to the provinces, and the fact that the legislation did not apply to the province of Quebec.
Then, we have on the order paper a resolution relating to the Canada pension plan. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has assured us that the plan the province of Quebec will pass will be in major respects similar to the proposed national Canada pension plan. But what will happen in the years to come? We have been assured that there will be complete portability between all provinces in so far as the pension is concerned. What will happen if five or 20 years from now the province of Quebec, which is the only province that so far has indicated it will opt out of that plan, makes changes within its own plan? How portable will the pension then be if the Quebec plan differs materially from the Canada pension plan that is created by a federal statute and then applies to the other nine provinces? These are problems that may well arise in the future.
When it comes to this question of opting out, not only are the provinces allowed to opt out of new programs proposed by this government, but this government is going one step farther and allowing the provinces to opt out of existing, well established and proven programs. The Prime Minister, in his letter of August 15, 1964, gives the provinces the right to opt out of hospital insurance, old age assistance, blind persons allowances, disabled persons allowance, unemployment assistance, vocational training, health grants and several others such as forestry agreements, hospital construction, roads to resources and so on. It seems to me that the need to strengthen some of these programs by action by the federal government is even greater today than at the time these programs were instituted. For example, there have been a number of briefs presented by the forest industry of British Columbia to the effect that the federal government should take more initiative in carrying out research in so far as forest fire protection is concerned. Yet the proposal of the present government is that these provinces could opt out of these forest agreements.
In this regard, Mr. Chairman, I should like to quote from an editorial in the Vancouver Province of October 24, 1964. The headline is, "Leading Canada toward the abyss". I read a part of this editorial:
From every part of Canada come indications that well-meaning peacemaker Lester Pearson is blandly and blindly leading the Canadian union

into a bottomless manhole.
I skip a part and I quote again:
This is supposed to mean a system of give and take between Ottawa and the provinces. But it is rapidly becoming a synonym for a division of this nation into a headless collection of minor principalities.
Again, I skip a part and continue to quote:
Canada is changing its constitution (the British North America Act) through secret conversations between Ottawa and the provincial governments. The public will be told what is good for it in pompously phrased communiques or in what leaks out from the secret meetings...
Canada is in danger of ceasing to be a nation in the truest sense of the word and becoming a collection of provinces divided by regional and racial interests having few common goals and interests.
Canada has stood united for nearly 100 years. It can fall apart in five if positive steps are not taken to avert such a tragedy. Already Premier Ross Thatcher of Saskatchewan has warned that his province would consider union with the U.S. if Quebec left confederation...
In all this the chief burden of responsibility falls on Mr. Pearson and his government. It is the national government, charged with leading, not following, the provinces. This demands toughness and steadiness, and more than a little of what Winston Churchill calls a "touch of the brute" on the part of Mr. Pearson.
"Co-operative federalism" sounds good. But it could be the death rattle of nationhood unless there is a great deal more federalism and a great deal less enthusiasm for the idea of subdividing our country into ten little satraps.
I am afraid that this government does not have this toughness to which this article refers, but they have demonstrated-
