Mr. Chairman, I wish to enter this debate briefly this evening to make a plea to the government on behalf of a group of Canadian citizens who I believe are not being fairly treated. This particular group is the federal civil service superannuates. My submission is on behalf of all of this group in general but especially on behalf of those who retired between the years 1952 and 1958.
My attention was drawn to this matter early this year when I and the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton met in Fredericton with the Fredericton branch of the federal superannuates national association and heard their submission. These men and women have rendered loyal and faithful service to our nation, and in a great many cases they are suffering severe hardship because of the meagre superannuation they are being paid.
I would like to quote from a letter dated April 13, 1964, signed by Mr. Fred W. White-

house, national secretary-treasurer of the federal superannuates national association, and addressed to the Prime Minister. I shall not read all of the letter, just the parts that are pertinent to the point I want to raise:
Under the Public Service Adjustment Act 1958-59, no person who retired under the five year plan after December 1959 and under the ten year plan after December 1952, received any benefits. E.g. an officer of the immigration branch who retired March 3, 1954 as an 1.0.7, received a salary for 1953 of $4,553.26, and his superannuation was computed on his last ten years of service, his salary in 1944 being $2,530. Had he retired the same day in 1964, he would have a rating of F.S.O.2 with a salary of $7,460 and superannuation would be computed on his last six years of service. This example applies throughout the service.
This particular group I have mentioned, those retiring between 1952 and 1958, are by far the worst off of all the superannuates. The letter goes on to say:
The United Kingdom increased pensions in 1952. 1956, 1959 and again in 1962. The commonwealth of Australia passed an act which came into effect November 13, 1963, granting increases to retired civil servants of that country. The government of the United States of America-
In which we are all deeply interested this evening.
__recognized the need for upward adjustment in
pensions of its retired federal personnel some years ago and made periodic upward adjustments. A bill was recently passed to provide an escalator clause in that pensions of retired federal personnel would automatically be adjusted when the cost of living showed an increase of 3 per cent or more.
We know your government is aware of what other countries throughout the world have done for their retired employees and, as pointed out in previous representations, Canada is sadly lacking in this respect.
We are not unmindful of the fact that our basic superannuation plan is considered one of the best, and we would like to keep it in that category. This cannot be done unless amendments are made in the Public Service Pension Adjustment Act which are so vitally necessary, as we have tried our utmost to point out to your government.
These are some figures quoted in this letter which amazed me:
According to the Public Accounts of Canada, March 31, 1963, volume I, page 167, the public service superannuation fund had an accumulated surplus at that date of $1,724,116,105-
Note that figure of $1 billion.
-an increase over the previous year of $137,187,000. I am requested to state once more it is the considered opinion of the superannuates of this country that an upward adjustment in their pensions could be made from the superannuation fund without cost to the general public when such a huge surplus has accumulated, as shown in the above figures.
As reported in the press this morning, the Civil Service Association of Canada took this
Interim Supply
matter up with the Prime Minister yesterday, and I would like to place on the record the press release which the association issued:
The Civil Service Association of Canada today released the text of a letter to Prime Minister Pearson calling for a review of civil service pensions. The letter to the Prime Minister cites the straitened circumstances of many pensioners and calls for a new policy of periodic pension review.
The C.S.A.C. wants the government to ensure that retired civil servants will have their pensions increased by a percentage equal to any salary adjustment for active civil servants. The association asks for a cyclical review of civil service pensions, every two years, as is now the case with salaries.
The association spokesman went on to say that his organization had made representation on many occasions seeking an equitable system for periodic pension review. In asking for a new government policy for pensioners the C.S.A.C. says:
We do not believe that we exaggerate in saying the situation of many pensioners is tragic.
Reviewing the developments of the past 20 years the C.S.A.C. notes that the purchasing power of the 1943 dollar has been reduced now to 56 cents and the association declares that it believes "some regular procedure of periodic pension adjustment is necessary." The actual resolution that was referred to reads as follows-and I wish to place it on the record for the benefit of hon. members interested in this problem:
Whereas in many cases, retired civil servants have been superannuated on the percentage of salary retirement, and
Whereas many of these retired civil servants, because of age, sickness or other reasons are unable to supplement their superannuation pay, and Whereas the cost of living has steadily risen and continues to rise, causing hardship to those who, after, in many cases, long and faithful service to the country are now living in very straitened circumstances with no consideration being given to adjusting pensions, when salary increases are being given or considered for government staffs, therefore
Be it resolved that the government implement on a regular two year cycle a review of pensions for all superannuated employees, and that pensions be adjusted in line with the percentage of salary increase granted employees during this period, and Be it further resolved that moneys to cover such increase be recovered from the general consolidated revenue fund.
There is also a table included which I will not put on the record but it emphasizes that the 1943 dollar is now worth only 56 cents.
I would therefore ask the government, and more specifically the Minister of Finance, who I regret is not here and neither is his parliamentary secretary-but I see the President of the Privy Council in his seat and I am sure he is deeply interested in this problem-

Interim Supply
to take action at once on behalf of these people, who I believe are being unfairly treated.
There are many problems facing our nation in this day and age. Some of them have been discussed during the last few days of this debate. There is the constitutional problem and a great many others such as the unrest in one of our founding provinces, a province in which I am deeply interested; the increase in crime, especially among juveniles in our larger cities; the impact of automation which is changing the whole pattern of employment, and the large number of Canadians we find who are without proper skills and education and who form the hard core of the unemployed.
But there is another problem that is pertinent to what I have been discussing this evening, the very insidious problem of inflation. Almost every monthly release of the dominion bureau of statistics shows an increase in the cost of living. The purchasing power of the dollar is going steadily downward year by year. Inflation falls especially heavily on those who are living on fixed incomes, particularly those who are living on small annuities and pensions. We know, of course, that over the past eight years old age pensions have been increased in several stages, from $40 until they now amount to $75 a month, and we are also aware that there have been corresponding increases in pensions to the blind, the disabled, and others. There remains the group of people about whom I have been speaking. I think more could be done for them by government, not only by this government but perhaps by the previous one, too. Those who have served this nation and who have retired on very small pensions, and upon whom the effects of inflation have fallen most heavily-these are the people upon whose behalf I have taken a few minutes of the time of the committee this evening.
